02.2Chapter 2 · The Base RAG Stack

Text Chunking

Chunking ek bade text string, jaise kisi document ka full text, ko chhote parts me todne ka process hai jinhe chunks kehte hain. Example ke liye, hum ek lambe article ko individual paragraphs ya sections me tod sakte hain, ya sentences me bhi. Chunking RAG ka ek necessary step hai — aur iske peeche teen bade reasons hain.

Pehla reason — LLM ki finite context window

Chunking ki primary reason LLM context window ki finite nature hai. Likhne ke samay state-of-the-art LLMs ki context windows kuch is tarah hain: ek leading model ki 400k tokens, aur do dusre leading models ki 1M tokens. Ye numbers bade lag sakte hain, lekin enterprise-grade tasks par ye deceptive abundance hain. Ek normal person lagbhag 120 words per minute bolta hai. Kyunki ek English word lagbhag 1.3 tokens hota hai, 400k ki context window lagbhag 42 hours ki continuous speech ke liye kaafi hai. Ye bahut lag sakta hai, lekin agar aapko kisi topic ke baare me market ka consensus chahiye saare relevant earnings calls ke transcripts ke basis par, to 42 hours simply kaafi nahi hai. Chunking context window me relevant information ki maximum amount pack karne me madad karta hai. Chunking ke through hum context window ko jitni zyada relevant information se bhar sakte hain, utna LLM complete picture ke saath response generate kar sakta hai. Earnings call wale example me, jahan context window saare earnings call transcripts accommodate karne ke liye kaafi lambi nahi hai, agar aapko sirf industry ke top 10 players me head counts ki growth ki parwah hai, to sirf us topic se related chunks hi context window me include honge. Revenue ya technological breakthroughs jaise dusre topics ke chunks exclude ho jayenge.

Latency aur cost — lamba context mehenga padta hai

Context window ki strict capacity constraints ke alawa, chunking ke liye ek compelling performance argument hai: computational overhead aur inference latency. Ek hardware vendor ke benchmark ne alag-alag context window lengths ke liye time to first token (TTFT) examine kiya — ek 70B parameter model, 2 high-end GPUs par. Result kuch is tarah tha: 200 tokens par 31 ms, 500 tokens par 47 ms, 1000 tokens par 82 ms, 5000 tokens par 406 ms, aur 10000 tokens par 1833 ms. Roughly estimate kiya jata hai ki transformer-based LLM ki inference time context length ke saath quadratically scale karti hai. Ye project karna reasonable hoga ki jab hum hundreds of thousands tokens ke kareeb pahunchenge, to TTFT unacceptably bad user experience dega. Ye experiments bahut luxurious configuration par hue the — ek single high-end GPU instance hi thousands of dollars per month cost karta hai. Context length ko chunking se kam karke inference latency aur cost ko significantly kam kiya ja sakta hai.

Dusra reason — embedding models ki chhoti context window

Chunking ka dusra rationale bhi context window se related hai, lekin is baar embedding models ki context window se. Embedding models text chunks ko vectors me convert karne ke liye use hote hain — vector database me store karne aur fast, semantic retrieval ke liye. Lekin unki context windows LLMs ki comparison me bahut chhoti hoti hain. State-of-the-art embedding models ki context window chhoti hai — example ke liye, ek leading provider ke third- aur fourth-generation embedding models ki context window 8k tokens hai, aur ek dusre provider ke second-generation embedding model ki bhi 8k hai. Isliye un cases me chunk size ko 8k tokens tak limit karna padta hai.

Teesra reason — response quality behtar hoti hai

Chunking ka teesra reason hai RAG ki response quality improve karna — retrieval aur generation dono stages par. Agar ek bada chunk multiple topics cover karta hai, to us bade chunk ka embedding vector har topic ko weakly reflect karta hai. Agar hum bade chunk ko chhote chunks me tod dein, to har chhota chunk ek topic par focus karega, aur is tarah uska embedding us topic ko behtar represent karega. Retrieval stage par iska matlab hai aapko higher-relevance chunks milte hain, aur generation stage par chhote chunks ka matlab hai LLM ko kam irrelevant information present ki jati hai, jisse zyada accurate responses milte hain. Ye widely acknowledge kiya jata hai ki LLMs ki reasoning ability context length badhne par degrade hoti hai. Example ke liye, ek provider ke 1M context announcement ka plot dikhata hai ki teen providers ke LLMs ki retrieval abilities context badhne par degrade hoti hain. Chhote chunks ke saath LLM irrelevant details se distract hue bina sabse relevant information par focus kar sakta hai.

Chunking strategies — paanch tareeke

  • Fixed-size chunking: sabse basic strategy — documents ko predefined size ke chunks me split karna, typically characters, words ya tokens me measure kiya jata hai. Iski primary limitation ye hai ki ye text ki natural structure ko disregard karta hai, aur sentences ya semantic units ko potentially split kar deta hai. Ek common mitigation hai overlapping chunks introduce karna, jahan ek chunk ke end ke tokens agle chunk ki shuruaat me repeat hote hain, taaki boundaries ke across local context preserve rahe.
  • Sentence- ya paragraph-based splitting (content-aware): ye approach text ko line breaks (jaise double newline) se paragraphs me ya sentence boundary detection rules (jaise punctuation) se sentences me segment karta hai. Sentence segmentation challenging hai, kai edge cases ki wajah se (jaise abbreviations jahan periods sentence boundaries denote nahi karte). Specialized tools — jinhe sentencizers ya sentence segmenters kehte hain — NLP libraries jaise spaCy, Stanza aur NLTK provide karte hain. Har resulting unit ek chunk ke roop me serve kar sakti hai. Agar single-sentence chunks bahut granular hain, to consecutive sentences merge ki ja sakti hain, aur context preserve karne ke liye chunks ke beech optional overlap rakha ja sakta hai.
  • Recursive chunking: ye approach delimiters ki hierarchy use karke text ko progressively chhoti units me split karta hai (jaise paragraphs → sentences → clauses). Ek representative implementation LangChain ka RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter hai.
  • Document-structure chunking: ye method recursive chunking ko extend karta hai — explicit document structure, jaise sections aur subsections, incorporate karke. Example ke liye, ek Markdown document ko heading levels (jaise # → ## → ###) ke basis par hierarchically segment kiya ja sakta hai, jisse content ki logical organization preserve rehti hai.
  • Semantic chunking: ye paradigm ko aage badhata hai — text ko semantic similarity ke basis par segment karke, jaise sentences ko topic ke according cluster karke. Is approach se semantically coherent chunks bante hain, sirf surface-level structure par rely karne ke bajaye.

Strategies ki tulna — pros aur cons

Fixed-size chunking implement karne me simple hai, predictable chunk size deti hai, aur indexing aur batching ke liye efficient hai — lekin semantic aur syntactic structure tod deti hai, sentences split kar sakti hai, aur context preserve karne ke liye overlap chahiye hota hai (jo redundancy add karta hai). Sentence/paragraph-based chunking linguistic structure preserve karti hai, zyada coherent chunks deti hai, aur NLP tools se implement karna aasan hai — lekin sentence boundary detection error-prone ho sakta hai, chunk sizes uneven ho jate hain, aur higher-level context abhi bhi miss ho sakta hai. Recursive chunking flexible hai, structure ke multiple levels par adapt karti hai, aur overly large ya small chunks avoid karti hai — lekin implement/tune karna zyada complex hai, delimiter quality par depend karti hai, aur true semantics ko abhi bhi ignore kar sakti hai. Document-structure chunking document ki logical organization se align hoti hai (sections, headings) aur hierarchical context preserve karti hai — lekin well-structured documents chahiye hote hain, unstructured text par kam effective hoti hai, aur implementation format (jaise Markdown, HTML) par depend karti hai. Semantic chunking semantically coherent chunks deti hai, behtar retrieval quality aur embedding-based search se alignment — lekin computationally expensive hai, embeddings/clustering chahiye hoti hai, chunk size less predictable hota hai, aur debug/tune karna mushkil hota hai.

Kaunsi strategy chunein? — apne dataset par evaluate karo

Kaunsi chunking strategy use karni hai, ye decide karna mushkil hai — koi ek rule nahi hai jo saare cases me best kaam kare. Ek common practice hai apne dataset ke basis par evaluate karna. Ek vector database provider ek example offer karta hai jise aap chunking strategy decide karte waqt refer kar sakte hain. Chunking effectiveness ko retrieval ya generation stage par evaluate kiya ja sakta hai. Retrieval ko usually retrieval benchmarks jaise BEIR par evaluate kiya jata hai, aur precision, recall, F1, nDCG (normalized discounted cumulative gain) aur MRR (mean reciprocal rank) jaise metrics me. Generation ko usually un benchmarks par evaluate kiya jata hai jinme given context/passages se answers dhoondhne hote hain, jaise question answering (QA) ya machine reading comprehension (MRC), aur BERTScore ya LLM-based judgment jaise metrics me. Dhyaan rahe ki LLM generation ki evaluation chunks ki ranking se affect ho sakti hai, kyunki LLMs shuruaat aur end me maujood chunks par zyada dhyaan dete hain — ise "lost in the middle" effect kehte hain. Isliye sirf generation evaluation ke basis par ye conclude mat karo ki ek chunking strategy dusri se behtar hai. LLM generation kai factors se impact ho sakti hai.

Surprising finding — semantic chunking hamesha behtar nahi

Somewhat surprisingly, aapko lag sakta hai ki saari chunking strategies similar performance deti hain aur koi ek strategy aapko sabse behtar performance nahi deti. Ek recent research paper — "Is Semantic Chunking Worth the Computational Cost?" — dikhata hai ki fixed-size chunking aur semantic chunking se BEIR aur RAGBench (retrieval task evaluate karne ke liye do industry-renowned benchmarks) par koi farq nahi padta. Lekin readers ko is conclusion ko definitive nahi manna chahiye — existing benchmarks pre-RAG time me banaye gaye the, aur is tarah usually short passages contain karte hain, aur chunking ka impact longer texts me zyada pronounced ho sakta hai. Zyada se zyada modern, RAG-specific benchmarks jo long passages contain karte hain, unke saath hum future me alag conclusions dekh sakte hain.

Code examples — kya karte hain (prose me)

Book me chunking ke do code examples hain. Pehla, spaCy ke sentencizer se: ek pre-trained English model load karke ek lambe text ko sentences me split kiya jata hai, aur har sentence ko print kiya jata hai. spaCy ka sentencizer punctuation se split karne ke comparison me edge cases ko behtar handle karta hai, jaise abbreviations ya titles jinme periods hote hain — example me ek sentence ke beech me question mark bhi use fool nahi kar pata. Dusra, Python ki native string operations se ek fixed-length chunker: chunk size 30 characters aur overlap 8 characters ke saath, text ko step size (chunk size minus overlap) se iterate karke chunks banaye jate hain. Is extreme example me output se obvious hai ki fixed-length chunking words tod deti hai, jisse embedding ke liye noise create hota hai. Lekin agar chunks kaafi lambe hain, to aise noises ka impact chhota hota hai — aur aise case me fixed-length chunking apni speed ke liye ek achha option hai.

Yaad rakho: Chunking ke teen reasons yaad rakho — LLM context window, latency/cost, aur embedding model ki chhoti window — aur quality ka fayda bonus hai. Koi universal best strategy nahi hai; apne dataset aur apne benchmarks par evaluate karo, aur "lost in the middle" effect ko yaad rakho.
SOURCESource: Hands-On RAG for Production, O'Reilly, Chapter 2 — The Base RAG Stack
← Previous02.1 · Document Parsing→ Next02.3 · Embedding Models
02.3Chapter 2 · The Base RAG Stack

Embedding Models

Maan lo aap apne documents se United States ke baare me saari information dhoondhna chahte hain. Ek initial approach hai saare chunks dhoondhna jinme "United States" words hain. Lekin ye approach "the U.S." ya "America" jaise phrases wale chunks miss kar degi, jo same entity ko refer karte hain lekin alag wording use karte hain. Aur zyada obvious example hoga "two" shabd ko number "2" se dhoondhne ki koshish karna. Is paragraph me dikhne wali challenge human languages ki ek fundamental characteristic ki wajah se hai: surface (dis)similarity semantic (dis)similarity se aligned nahi hoti. Ek word ki spelling ek concept ka surface form hai. Similar surface forms wale do words, jaise "hat" aur "mat", necessarily semantically similar nahi hote ya same ya similar concepts refer nahi karte. Surface (dis)similarity aur semantic (dis)similarity ke beech ye misalignment artificial intelligence aur khaas taur par natural language processing ki ek lambe samay se thorny problem rahi hai. Yahi woh jagah hai jahan embedding models aate hain.

Embedding kya hai?

Embedding ka process textual data (RAG ke context me ya to ek retrieved chunk ya user ki query) ko floating point numbers ke vector me map karta hai, jise embedding vector ya simply embedding kehte hain. Ye vectors text ke semantic meaning ko capture karte hain, jisse effective comparison aur retrieval possible hoti hai jo simple keyword matching achieve nahi kar sakti. Do semantically similar phrases (jaise "Uncle Sam" aur "US Government") ke embedding vectors ke beech distance chhoti hogi, despite quite different spelling. Vector distance ko efficiently compute kiya ja sakta hai dot product jaise operations se, jin ke liye aaj ke GPUs optimize hain. Embedding ek bottleneck solve karta hai jo NLP ko saalon se pareshan kar raha tha: surface dissimilarity par semantic similarity capture karna (jaise "Uncle Sam" versus "US Government") aur surface similarity par semantic dissimilarity (jaise "cat" versus "hat"). Agar query me "Uncle Sam" hai aur hum sirf words ke surface form par rely karte hain, to hum "US Government" phrase wale chunks miss kar denge aur "Uncle Tom" ya "Uncle Bob" wale chunks ko prefer bhi kar sakte hain, jo semantically irrelevant hain. Embedding ka purpose hai textual data ko represent karne ka aisa tareeka dhoondhna ki representation me similarity semantic similarity se align kare. Kyunki aise embeddings usually ek neural network train karke obtain kiye jate hain, aise representations ko aksar dense representation kehte hain, aur in embeddings par based retriever ko kabhi-kabhi dense retriever kehte hain.

Embedding sirf synonyms ke liye nahi hai

"Uncle Sam" versus "US Government" wale example se ye galat impression mat lo ki embedding sirf synonyms match karne ke liye hai — matlab same meaning wale words. Example ke liye, agar query hai "Find all cases that happened in the US" aur aapka data source sirf state names mention karta hai jaise California ya Alberta (jo ek Canadian province hai), to sahi embeddings ke saath model California wale cases retrieve kar sakta hai, jabki Alberta wale ignore kar dega.

Thoda itihaas — one-hot se Word2Vec se BERT tak

Words ko vectors ke roop me represent karna natural language processing me ek long-standing problem raha hai. 1990s me recurrent neural networks par ek influential kaam me one-hot encoding use kiya gaya tha words represent karne ke liye. One-hot encoding me har word ko vocabulary ke size ke barabar length wale vector ke roop me represent kiya jata hai, jisme saare elements zero set hote hain, sirf ek element ke alawa jo vocabulary me word ke index se correspond karta hai aur one set hota hai. Asli breakthrough 2010s me deep learning ke advent ke saath aaya. 2013 me ek mashhoor Word2Vec model introduce hua, jo ek word ko vector me map karta hai ek simple task ke through — ek target word dekar surrounding words predict karna, jise skip-gram model kehte hain. Example ke liye, sentence "I had pizza for lunch" me beech wala word "pizza" dekar, woh "I", "had", "for" aur "lunch" words predict karta hai. Result exciting tha. Famously, "queen" aur "woman" ke beech vector difference "king" aur "man" ke beech wale ke lagbhag parallel dikhaya gaya tha. Aise embeddings ko "static embeddings" kehte hain — "static" is sense me ki training ke baad har word ka embedding fixed hota hai. 2018 me ek transformer-based model ke introduction ne field ko aur aage badhaya — contextualized embeddings ya "dynamic embeddings" enable karke, jo ek word ka embedding uske context ke basis par determine karte hain. Precisely bolen to, embed words nahi, tokens hote hain — meanings ko zyada precisely capture karne ke liye modern approaches kabhi-kabhi words ko subword tokens me tod deti hain, jaise "geopolitical" ko "geo" aur "political" me.

Selection criteria — size, dimensions, context window

Kisi bhi machine learning model ki tarah, embedding model select karte waqt pehla trade-off jo aapko karna padta hai woh hai model size aur uski performance. Ek bada model semantics ko behtar characterize kar sakta hai lekin slower bhi ho sakta hai aur zyada memory chahiye hogi. Aap ek benchmark use karke balance dhoondh sakte hain. Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) embedding models ki performance evaluate karne ke liye ek industry benchmark hai; aap MTEB Leaderboard par embedding models ki rankings dekh sakte hain. Embedding dimensions ek aur important factor hai. Higher-dimensional embeddings zyada nuanced semantic information capture kar sakte hain, lekin unhe zyada computational resources bhi chahiye hote hain. Specific use case ke basis par dimensionality aur efficiency ke beech balance dhoondhna essential hai. Kai embedding models, jaise ek leading provider ke embedders aur ek dusre provider ke Gemini embedders, aapko embedding vector ko simply truncate karke embeddings ki dimensionality adjust karne dete hain. Ye embedder ki training process ke dauraan ek technique se achieve hota hai jise Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) kehte hain, jo loss function ko alag-alag dimensions par embedding ke losses ke sum ke roop me design karke sabse discriminative semantic information ko lower dimensions me push karta hai. Jabki MRL kisi bhi point par truncation allow karta hai, standard practice hai power-of-two subdimensions use karna (jaise full vector ka 1/8, 1/4 ya 1/2), kyunki model usually training process ke dauraan in specific dimensional granularities par optimize hota hai. LLMs ki tarah, jin ki context windows hoti hain, embedding models ki bhi input size par limitations hoti hain. Likhne ke samay representative embedding models ki context window (tokens ki sankhya me) kuch is tarah hai: ek provider ke Qwen3-Embedding models ki 32k, ek leading provider ke third-generation text-embedding-3 models ki 8k, ek dusre provider ke second-generation embedding model ki 8k, aur ek research institute ke BGE-M3 model ki 1k.

Practical tips aur considerations

  • Chunking ko embedding model ki context window se match karo: agar aapke chunks model ki context window se lambe hain, to zyadaatar serving frameworks, jaise ek popular transformers library, chunks ko silently truncate kar denge, jisse information loss aur degraded retrieval hoga.
  • Embedding dimensions aapke vector DB ki requirements meet karein: example ke liye, pgvector 32-bit, full-precision floatpoint embeddings ke liye dimension ko 2,000 par cap karta hai.
  • Precision kam karke storage aur computation bachao: embeddings ki precision kam karna ek common practice hai — jaise 16-bit floats ya 8-bit integers tak. Kai serving frameworks ya SaaS endpoints aapko woh precision specify karne dete hain jo aap returning embeddings ke liye chahte hain.
  • JSON inefficient hai, Base64 use karo: embedding endpoints typically JSON format me vectors return karte hain, jo numerical data ke liye notoriously inefficient hai. Ek single 8-bit integer jaise "123" binary me sirf 1 byte chahiye, lekin JSON string ke roop me 3 bytes consume karta hai. Iske alawa, JSON ke through floats transmit karne se string serialization ke dauraan precision loss ka risk hota hai. Ise solve karne ke liye kai platforms Base64 encoding support karte hain; jabki ye full floating-point precision preserve karta hai aur payload size kam karta hai, iske liye client side par original float array restore karne ke liye ek decoding step chahiye hota hai.

Code example — Sentence Transformers se embeddings

Sentence Transformers effective sentence embeddings produce karne ke liye ek architecture hai, aur uska Python package kai pre-trained embedding models provide karta hai. Book me iska use karke demonstrate kiya gaya hai ki embeddings kaise kaam karte hain. Pehle libraries import karke model load kiya jata hai — ek chhota pre-trained model, all-MiniLM-L6-v2. Phir chaar sample sentences embed ki jati hain: "I am a happy person.", "I am a joyful person.", "I am a pessimistic person.", aur "I am not an optimistic person." Embeddings ka shape (4, 384) hota hai — matlab chaar sentences, har ek ki 384-dimensional embeddings. Phir sentences ke beech pairwise similarity compute ki jati hai. Similarity matrix me diagonal elements har sentence ki khud se similarity hote hain, jo hamesha 1 hoti hai. Pehli sentence ki dusri sentence se similarity 0.8151 hai — kaafi high, jo indicate karta hai ki do sentences semantically similar hain. Teesri aur chauthe sentences se uski similarity 0.3864 aur 0.5210 hai — lower semantic similarity. Aakhri do rows ko dekhne par, teesri sentence chauthe sentence se sabse similar hai, 0.7047 score ke saath, jabki pehli aur dusri sentences se uski similarity 0.3864 aur 0.3383 hai — kaafi low. Ise heatmap ke roop me visualize bhi kiya jata hai.

Ek interesting experiment — random dimensions bhi kaam karte hain

Phir ek interesting experiment kiya jata hai: embeddings ka randomly ek slice lekar unki similarities compute karna. Ek run me dimensions 67 se 158 use kiye gaye, aur similarity matrix ne full embeddings se mile pattern jaisa hi pattern dikhaya — sentences 1 aur 2 abhi bhi sabse similar hain, phir sentences 3 aur 4. Agar aap process ko alag random dimensions se repeat karte hain, to aapko similarity matrices me similar patterns observe honge. Ye indicate karta hai ki aaj ke embedding models itne achhe hain ki embedding space ka randomly selected subspace bhi meaningful semantic relationships capture kar sakta hai.

Yaad rakho: Embedding ka kaam hai surface form ko semantic meaning me badalna — "United States", "USA" aur "America" ek hi jagah point karein, aur "cat" aur "hat" alag rahen. Model chunte waqt size, dimensions (MRL se truncate kar sakte ho) aur context window — teeno ko apne chunks aur vector DB se match karo.
embedding.ipynb — Sentence Embeddings and Similarity — GitHub: ofermend/hands-on-rag, chapter2/embedding.ipynb (https://github.com/ofermend/hands-on-rag/blob/main/chapter2/embedding.ipynb)
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import random 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Load the pre-trained Sentence Transformer model
model = SentenceTransformer('all-MiniLM-L6-v2')

# List of sentences to encode
sentences = [
    "I am a happy person.",
    "I am a joyful person.",
    "I am a pessimistic person.",
    "I am not an optimistic person."
]

# Generate embeddings for the sentences
embeddings = model.encode(sentences)

# Let's take a look at the embeddings

print (embeddings.shape)
print (embeddings[:, :5]) # only first 5 dimension due to space constraints

# compute the cosine similarity between the embeddings
similarity_matrix = model.similarity(embeddings, embeddings)
print (similarity_matrix)

# visualize the similarity matrix using heatmap 

plt.figure(figsize=(5, 5))
plt.imshow(similarity_matrix, cmap='RdYlGn_r', interpolation='nearest', vmin=0, vmax=1)
plt.title('Cosine Similarity between any pair of embeddings')
plt.xlabel('Sentence ID')
plt.ylabel('Sentence ID')
plt.xticks([0, 1, 2, 3])
plt.yticks([0, 1, 2, 3])

# Add text annotations
for i in range(len(similarity_matrix)):
    for j in range(len(similarity_matrix)):
        plt.text(j, i, f'{similarity_matrix[i][j]:.3f}', 
                ha='center', va='center', color='black')

plt.show()

# compute the cosine similarity between the embeddings between two random semantic dimensions

# generate two random integers between 0 and 384
rand1 = random.randint(0, 384)
rand2 = random.randint(0, 384)

if rand1 > rand2:
    rand1, rand2 = rand2, rand1

print (f"Using semantic dimensions {rand1} to {rand2}")

similarity_matrix = model.similarity(embeddings[:, rand1:rand2], embeddings[:, rand1:rand2])
print (similarity_matrix)
SOURCESource: Hands-On RAG for Production, O'Reilly, Chapter 2 — The Base RAG Stack

02.4Chapter 2 · The Base RAG Stack

Vector Databases and Vector Search

Text ko embeddings me convert karna effective retrieval ki taraf sirf pehla step hai. Agla step hai in embeddings ko aise store karna jo quick similarity lookups allow kare. Yahi woh jagah hai jahan vector databases aati hain.

Vector-based similarity search samajhna

Embedding ki beauty ye hai ki do embeddings ke beech vector difference un do pieces of text ke beech semantic similarity reflect karta hai jinhe embeddings represent karte hain. Vector similarity measure karne ka ek common approach hai dot product. Dot product jitna zyada hoga, do vectors aur unke corresponding texts semantically utne hi similar honge. Dhyaan rahe ki dot products se semantic similarities compare karte waqt hum vector magnitude ke influence ko remove kar sakte hain, taaki sirf do embeddings ke beech angular difference consider ho. Isliye embeddings ko normalize karna padta hai — matlab magnitude 1 ho. Jab vectors normalize hote hain, to unka dot product ek dusre concept ke barabar hota hai, jise cosine similarity kehte hain. Query ki embedding dekar, query se sabse relevant chunks dhoondhne ka ek naive lekin brute-force approach hoga database me saare embedding vectors ke saath query embedding ka dot product compute karna. Is tarah complexity O(n) hoti hai, jahan n database me vectors ki sankhya hai. Jab aapka data chhota hai, to brute force approach theek kaam kar sakta hai. Aapka setup itna simple ho sakta hai jitna saare pre-ingested vectors ko RAM me store karna. Lekin millions ya billions chunks wale bade-scale production deployment ke liye hume brute force se smarter approach chahiye. Achhi khabar ye hai ki hume database ke saare vectors ke saath dot products compute karne ki zaroorat nahi hai, agar hum chhoti errors tolerate karne ko taiyaar hain. Ye hai approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search ka idea. Iske contrast me, brute force approach ko kabhi-kabhi exact nearest neighbors (ENN) ya FlatIndex search bhi kehte hain.

Approximate nearest neighbor algorithms — HNSW

Vector search ko speed up karne ke liye, lagbhag saare vector databases ya traditional relational database management systems (RDBMSs) ya NoSQL databases me vector search plug-ins kisi na kisi form me ANN algorithm offer karte hain. ANN me "approximate" shabd ka matlab hai ki algorithm exact nearest neighbor dhoondhne ki guarantee nahi deta, balki ek close enough neighbor deta hai. Sabse prominent ANN algorithm hai Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW). HNSW ek multi-layer structure banata hai jisme har vector same layer ke andar nearby vectors se connect hota hai. Upper layers me vectors ki chhoti sankhya hoti hai aur woh dataset ke coarse views represent karte hain, jabki lower layers me zyada vectors hote hain aur finer detail enable karte hain. Querying top se shuru hoti hai aur neeche ki taraf move karti hai, har level par hamesha un vectors tak pahunchne ki koshish karti hai jo query ke kareeb hain.

HNSW ko ek analogy se samjho — US cities

Ise intuitive banane ke liye, imagine karo ki aapko diye gaye coordinate ke nearest US city dhoondhni hai, jo California ke ek chhote shahar me hai. Brute-force approach desh ke har city ki distances calculate karega. HNSW iske bajaye layers me proceed karta hai. Top level par hum query ko sirf do major landmark cities ke against evaluate karte hain — Los Angeles aur New York City. Jo bhi kareeb hai, woh strong hint deta hai ki aage kahan search karna hai. Maan lo query Los Angeles ke kareeb hai. Phir hum agle level par move karte hain aur query ko western United States ke kai bade cities — Los Angeles khud, San Francisco, Seattle, Denver — ke against compare karte hain. Agar San Francisco sabse kareeb nikla, to hum Northern California me zoom karte hain. Phir hum neeche descend karte hain aur sirf Bay Area ke andar cities — San Francisco khud, Oakland, San Jose — compare karte hain. Maan lo San Jose is level par nearest hai. Hum aur neeche move karte hain, ab individual South Bay cities — Palo Alto, Sunnyvale, Mountain View, San Jose khud — evaluate karte hain. Jab tak hum sabse lowest level par pahunchenge, candidate cities extremely local honge, aur humne nearest match locate kar liya hoga — har step par sirf handful cities ki distances compute karke, desh ke har city ki nahi. Ye progressively refined search — pehle coarse, phir fine — hi hai jo HNSW ko practice me itna efficient banati hai. Kyunki HNSW graph ke through greedily navigate karta hai, ye abhi bhi possible hai — halanki rare hai — ki search "galat" region me kheench liya jaye, agar starting decision thoda off ho, jaise jab query do major metropolitan areas ke beech boundary par ho. Aise cases me HNSW ek aisa city return kar sakta hai jo true nearest city ke extremely close hai, lekin absolute mathematically closest nahi hai. Yehi ANN me "approximate" ka essence hai. Badle me, HNSW superb performance deta hai: woh dataset ka sirf ek chhota fraction examine karta hai, jabki accuracy zyadaatar practical applications me exact search ke lagbhag identical hoti hai — lekin computational cost ke ek fraction par. HNSW implement karne wali ek famous open source library hai ek bade social media company ki similarity search library, FAISS — jo HNSW aur dusre ANN algorithms ka highly optimized implementation provide karti hai, jisse developers ke liye apni applications me ANN search capabilities integrate karna aasan ho jata hai.

Vector databases — sirf search se zyada

Ek vector database ek aisa system hai jo high-dimensional embeddings manage, store aur query karne ke liye bana hai, aur primarily scalable form me ANN implement karta hai. Lekin vector databases sirf similar vectors search karne se aage jati hain, aur broader database concerns handle karti hain: persistence, updates, deletes, metadata management, filtering, scalability aur dusre systems ke saath integration. Historically, specialized vector databases mainstream databases se pehle emerge hue jinhone strong vector indexing offer ki; aaj kai general-purpose databases bhi vector search support karte hain. Example ke liye, PostgreSQL ke liye pgvector, SQLite ke liye sqlite-vec, aur MongoDB ke liye Atlas Vector Search. Isliye aaj hum simply ye nahi maan sakte ki vector DBs sirf vector search karte hain jabki traditional RDBMSs ya NoSQL databases sirf nonvector search karte hain. Kai vector DB systems, jaise proprietary Pinecone aur open source Milvus, Weaviate aur Qdrant, metadata filtering support karte hain, jo embeddings par perform nahi hoti, balki embeddings se associated metadata par hoti hai, jaise document IDs, timestamps, ya dusre attributes. Metadata sirf fields hain (traditional RDBMS ya NoSQL database me columns jaise), aur is tarah metadata filtering traditional database filtering jaisa operation perform karti hai. Halanki metadata filtering vector embeddings par perform nahi hoti, phir bhi ye vector search ki speed aur quality par impact daal sakti hai. Example ke liye, maan lo aapke paas decades se saari public companies ki quarterly financial reports hain. Agar aap ek specific company ke baare me specific period of time me questions poochna chahte hain, to DB system ke liye behtar hai ki woh pehle data ko company name aur time period dono se filter karke search space narrow kare, uske baad vector search kare — jo traditional filtering se bahut zyada expensive aur slow hai. Metadata filtering vector search se pehle, uske parallel me, aur uske baad ki ja sakti hai. Upar describe kiya gaya example pre-filtering hai. Metadata filtering aur vector search ko jointly perform karne wale algorithms bhi hain.

Vector search use karte waqt parameters — k aur dimensions

RAG pipeline me vector search ka ek key parameter hai return karne wale results ki sankhya, jise commonly k se denote kiya jata hai. k ki value na bahut chhoti ho sakti hai na bahut badi: agar k bahut chhota hai, to user query ka asal jawab miss ho sakta hai, kyunki woh k se aage rank ho sakta hai. Agar k bahut bada hai, to hume kai issues face karne pad sakte hain: pehle, hum LLM ki context window length exceed kar sakte hain; phir, hum noise aur irrelevant information introduce karke generation quality degrade kar sakte hain; aur aakhir me, hum generation step ki cost aur latency unnecessarily badha sakte hain. Pehle humne Matryoshka Representation Learning ka zikr kiya tha, jo users ko arbitrary embedding dimensions chunne ki flexibility deta hai. Reduced dimension vector database ka size kam karega aur vector search ko speed up karega. Lekin dimension ko bahut zyada kam karne se vector search ki quality degrade ho sakti hai. Balance point specific use case aur use kiye gaye embedding model par depend karta hai. Apne vector DB support karne wali maximal embedding dimensions ka dhyaan rakho. Example ke liye, pgvector 32-bit, full-precision floats ke liye 2,000 dimensions tak support karta hai.

Code example — pgvector se vectors store aur retrieve karna

pgvector ek extension hai jo PostgreSQL me vector search support add karta hai. Book me iske key steps dikhaye gaye hain. Pehle, Sentence Transformers se kuch sentences embed ki jati hain — wahi chaar sample sentences ("I am a happy person." aadi) — aur embeddings 2D NumPy arrays hote hain, jahan har row ek sentence ki embedding se correspond karti hai aur har column ek embedding dimension se. Phir, sentence_embeddings naam ki table banayi jati hai, jis me do columns hain: sentence aur embedding. Pehle pgvector extension enable ki jati hai, phir table create ki jati hai jisme embedding column ki dimension 384 specify ki jati hai — kyunki all-MiniLM-L6-v2 ki embedding dimension 384 hai. Ant me table me ek HNSW index create kiya jata hai, jo is table par efficient search facilitate karta hai, kuch parameters ke saath. Phir precomputed embeddings ko table me insert kiya jata hai — ek-ek karke SQL INSERT statement se. NumPy arrays ko insert karte waqt har row ko floats ki list me convert karke string me serialize karna padta hai, taaki INSERT statement properly form ho. Table ki contents dekhne par har sentence ke saath uske embedding ke pehle kuch values dikhte hain. Aakhir me, vector search ke liye ek function banaya jata hai: query ko embed kiya jata hai, phir SQL SELECT statement me cosine distance operator ka use karke sabse similar sentences dhoondhi jati hain, similarity score ke saath, aur top-k results limit kiye jate hain. pgvector me distance operator asal me do vectors ke beech dissimilarity measure karta hai, isliye similarity measure karne ke liye uska complement use karna padta hai. Example queries se ye clear hota hai: "I am a smiling person." query par "I am a happy person." (0.764) aur "I am a joyful person." (0.693) sabse upar aate hain, jabki "I am not an optimistic person." (0.384) bahut peeche hota hai. Dusri query "I have a bad feeling about the future." par "I am a pessimistic person." (0.561) aur "I am not an optimistic person." (0.506) upar aate hain, aur "I am a happy person." (0.322) peeche — bilkul sense banata hai.

Yaad rakho: Brute force O(n) hai — chhote data ke liye theek, bade data ke liye nahi. HNSW coarse-to-fine layers me search karke almost exact accuracy deta hai, fraction cost par. Aur k ko soch-samajh kar chuno — bahut chhota ho to jawab miss, bahut bada ho to noise, cost aur latency badhegi.
pgvector-simple.ipynb — Vector Search with pgvector — GitHub: ofermend/hands-on-rag, chapter2/pgvector-simple.ipynb (https://github.com/ofermend/hands-on-rag/blob/main/chapter2/pgvector-simple.ipynb)
from typing import List
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

model = SentenceTransformer('all-MiniLM-L6-v2')

sentences = [
    "I am a happy person.",
    "I am a joyful person.",
    "I am a pessimistic person.",
    "I am not an optimistic person."
]
embeddings = model.encode(sentences)

import psycopg2
import os

# Database connection parameters
pg_password = os.environ.get('PGVECTOR_PASSWORD', 'RAGBOOK')
DB_CONFIG = {
    'host': 'localhost',
    'port': 5432,
    'user': 'postgres',
    'password': pg_password,
    'database': 'postgres'  # Connect to default database first
}

# Connect to PostgreSQL
conn = psycopg2.connect(**DB_CONFIG)
conn.autocommit = True
cursor = conn.cursor()

DB_FOR_VECTORS = "ragbook" # lowercase only, use a non-default database for our experiments

# Create a database if it doesn't exist
try: 
    cursor.execute(f"CREATE DATABASE {DB_FOR_VECTORS};")
except psycopg2.errors.DuplicateDatabase:
    print (f'Database {DB_FOR_VECTORS} already exists.')

# Switch to the new database
DB_CONFIG['database'] = DB_FOR_VECTORS
conn = psycopg2.connect(**DB_CONFIG)
conn.autocommit = True
cursor = conn.cursor()  # Create a new cursor connecting to the new db `DB_FOR_VECTORS`

# Create a table for storing vectors

# Enable PG-Vector extension
cursor.execute("CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;")

# Drop the table if it already exists
cursor.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS sentence_embeddings;")

# Create a table called `sentence_embeddings`
cursor.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sentence_embeddings (
        text TEXT NOT NULL,
        embedding VECTOR(384)  -- all-MiniLM-L6-v2 produces 384-dimensional embeddings
    );
""")

# Create HNSW index in the table `sentence_embeddings` for efficient similarity search
cursor.execute("""
    CREATE INDEX 
    ON sentence_embeddings 
    USING hnsw (embedding vector_l2_ops) 
    WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64);
""")

# Insert sample sentences and their embeddings into the table `sentence_embeddings`

for sentence, embedding in zip(sentences, embeddings):
        embedding_as_list: List[float] = embedding.tolist()
        cursor.execute(
            "INSERT INTO sentence_embeddings (text, embedding) VALUES (%s, %s::vector)",
            (sentence, embedding_as_list)
        )

# Take a sneak peek at the table contents
cursor.execute("SELECT text, embedding FROM sentence_embeddings;")
rows = cursor.fetchall()
for row in rows:
    print(row)

# Embed a query and find the most similar sentence in the database

def vector_search(query, model, top_k):
    query_embedding = model.encode([query])[0]
    query_embedding_as_list: List[float] = query_embedding.tolist()

    cursor.execute(
            """
            SELECT text, 
                    1 - (embedding <=> %s::vector) as similarity
            FROM sentence_embeddings
            WHERE embedding IS NOT NULL
            ORDER BY embedding <=> %s::vector
            LIMIT %s;
            """,
            (query_embedding_as_list, query_embedding_as_list, top_k)
        )

    results = cursor.fetchall()

    for row in results:
        print(row)

query = "I am a smiling person."
vector_search(query, model, 3)

query = "I have a bad feeling about the future."
vector_search(query, model, 3)
sqlite-vec.ipynb — SQLite Vector Search with sqlite-vec — GitHub: ofermend/hands-on-rag, chapter2/sqlite-vec.ipynb (https://github.com/ofermend/hands-on-rag/blob/main/chapter2/sqlite-vec.ipynb)
from typing import List
import struct

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import sqlite3, sqlite_vec

# Load the pre-trained Sentence Transformer model
model = SentenceTransformer('all-MiniLM-L6-v2')
embedding_dimension = model.get_sentence_embedding_dimension()

# Prepare SQLite database
sqlite_db = sqlite3.connect('embeddings.db')
sqlite_db.enable_load_extension(True)
sqlite_vec.load(sqlite_db)
sqlite_db.enable_load_extension(False)


# List of sentences to encode
sentences = [
    "I am a happy person.",
    "I am a joyful person.",
    "I am a pessimistic person.",
    "I am not an optimistic person."
]

# Generate embeddings for the sentences
embeddings = model.encode(sentences, normalize_embeddings=True)

# Create the table 
sqlite_db.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS chunks")
sql_create_table = f"CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE chunks USING vec0(chunk_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, text TEXT, embedding float[{embedding_dimension}])"
sqlite_db.execute(sql_create_table)
sqlite_db.commit()

# Insert embeddings and their text into `chunks`

def serialize_f32(vector: List[float]) -> bytes:
    """serializes a list of floats into a compact "raw bytes" format"""
    return struct.pack("%sf" % len(vector), *vector)

for i, (text, embedding) in enumerate(zip(sentences, embeddings)):
    sql_insert = f"INSERT INTO chunks (chunk_id, text, embedding) VALUES (?, ?, ?)"
    sqlite_db.execute(sql_insert, (i, text, serialize_f32(embedding)))
sqlite_db.commit()

# Search using the embedding of a new sentence 

query = "I am a glad person."
query_embedding = model.encode(query, normalize_embeddings=True)

sql_select = f"SELECT chunk_id, text, embedding, distance FROM chunks WHERE embedding MATCH '{query_embedding.tolist()}' ORDER BY distance LIMIT 1"
cursor = sqlite_db.execute(sql_select)
results = cursor.fetchall()
for chunk_id, text, embedding, distance in results:
    print(f"Chunk ID: {chunk_id}, Text: {text}, Distance: {distance}")

# Search using the embedding of a new sentence 

query = "I am a negative person."
query_embedding = model.encode(query, normalize_embeddings=True)

sql_select = f"SELECT chunk_id, text, embedding, distance FROM chunks WHERE embedding MATCH '{query_embedding.tolist()}' ORDER BY distance LIMIT 1"
cursor = sqlite_db.execute(sql_select)
results = cursor.fetchall()
for chunk_id, text, embedding, distance in results:
    print(f"Chunk ID: {chunk_id}, Text: {text}, Distance: {distance}")

02.5Chapter 2 · The Base RAG Stack

Generative LLMs + Prompt Engineering

Ab hum RAG stack ke final step par hain: retrieved text chunks aur original user query ko ek LLM me feed karke ek response generate karna. Ye step ek text-to-text transform hai. Halanki pichhle vector search step me hum numerical embedding vectors par operate karte hain, hum embeddings ko LLM ko nahi bhejte. Iske bajaye, hum ek full LLM prompt bhejte hain, jisme instructions aur retrieved embeddings se correspond karne wale original text chunks shamil hote hain, aur LLM ek textual response ke saath respond karta hai.

LLMs — RAG me unke do sabse common tasks

LLMs RAG ke liye vital hain, kyunki unme context ko analyze aur reason karke human-like text generate karne ki ability hoti hai. RAG me LLMs ke do sabse common tasks hain — summarization (retrieved chunks ki coherent lekin concise rewriting) aur question answering (retrieved chunks ke basis par user query ka answer generate karna). LLMs in purposes ke liye ek achha tool hain, kyunki LLMs ko aisa output text generate karne ke liye train kiya jata hai jo user intents ki wide range ke according input text se relevant ho. Summarization aur question answering happen to be do sabse common user intents hain. Un par bahut saara training data devote kiya gaya hai, aur LLM vendors ne in functions me bahut effort invest kiya hai.

Inference speed — bottleneck aur use tez karne ke tareeke

Neural network use karke output produce karne ko inference kehte hain. Inference speed usually LLMs use karne me ek bottleneck hoti hai, khaas taur par jab aapka RAG system on-prem ya air-gapped environment me chalta hai, aur is tarah aapko LLM khud serve karna padta hai. Inference speed improve karne ke liye kai techniques develop ki gayi hain. Example ke liye: quantization LLM throughput ko speed up karti hai precision ko 32-bit (float32) se 16-bit (jaise float16 ya bfloat16 representation), 8-bit (int8), ya 4-bit (int4) tak kam karke. FlashAttention transformer-based LLMs ki inference accelerate karne ka ek popular method hai — attention values compute karte waqt memory usage ko zyada efficient banakar. vLLM aur Ollama jaise open source serving frameworks LLM inference accelerate karte hain aur hardware footprints kam karte hain — methods ke combination ko implement karke.

LLM chunna — speed vs quality, aur privacy

LLMs pick karte waqt speed aur quality ke beech ek trade-off hota hai. Generally, ek bada LLM ek chhote LLM se zyada capacities rakhta hai aur complex tasks par behtar results produce kar sakta hai. Lekin aksar task itna simple hota hai ki bada LLM sirf marginally behtar perform karta hai ya chhote LLM ke barabar hota hai. Aise case me bade LLM se aane wali latency aur cost justify karna mushkil hota hai. Ek evaluation set of data banane me effort lagana worth hai, taaki woh sweet-spot LLM dhoondha ja sake jo minimal cost par aapki expectation satisfy kare. LLMs pick karte waqt ek aur factor hai data privacy. Kai RAG use cases me on-premises ya air-gapped deployment chahiye hoti hai, matlab data public Internet par nahi ja sakta. Aise cases me proprietary LLMs ko public HTTP endpoints ke through use karna allowed nahi hota, aur zyadaatar developers ke liye open source LLMs hi ek option hote hain. Likhne ke samay, common RAG tasks, jaise summarization aur question answering, par open source aur proprietary LLMs ke beech gap kaafi chhota hai, aur rule of thumb hai ki 70B parameters se zyada wala ek open source LLM decent enough hota hai.

RAG prompt engineering — instruction following ki power

LLMs ki ek great power hai instruction following — matlab unhe prompt me di gayi instructions ke basis par specific tasks perform karne ke liye guide kiya ja sakta hai. Prompt engineering in prompts ko design aur refine karne ki practice hai, taaki model se desired responses elicit kiye ja sakein. RAG ke context me, retrieved results aur user query ko properly assemble karna padta hai, taaki LLM ko relevant response generate karne me guide kiya ja sake. Aisa karne ka koi absolute best tareeka nahi hai, kyunki ye specific use case aur use kiye ja rahe LLM par depend kar sakta hai. Yahan kuch examples hain jo readers ko apne prompt templates develop karne me inspire karenge.

Prompt templates — basic se behtar tak

Ek straightforward prompt template kuch is tarah hai: "You are a helpful information-processing assistant. Extract answers related to a search query based on the context provided. Here is the context: {retrieved_results}. Here is the search query: {query}." Yaad rakho, query flow me humne original user query ko retrieval query me rewrite karne ka zikr kiya tha. Ab jab hum generation step par hain, to hum yahan original user query use kar sakte hain — isse LLM ko aisa response generate karne me madad milegi jo user ke intent se zyada aligned hai. Lekin zyadaatar LLMs behtar perform kar sakte hain agar query ko context se pehle rakha jaye, unke training data ki wajah se. Isliye is tarah ka template prefer kiya ja sakta hai: pehle search query, phir context. Ek modern LLM ke paas complex reasoning karke khud ko behtar answers tak pahunchane ki ability hoti hai. Isliye aap prompt me aisi instructions add karna chahenge jo model ko uski reasoning capabilities leverage karne me madad karein. Example ke liye, aap prompt me ek simple chain-of-thought (CoT) instruction add kar sakte hain: "If the answer is not obviously present in the context, please think step by step and provide a detailed explanation of your reasoning process." Kyunki hallucination ek badi concern hai, aap LLM ko explicitly ye bhi keh sakte hain ki woh context me maujood information se adhere kare — prompt template me aisi instruction add karke: "If an answer cannot be reasonably inferred from the context, please simply say 'I don't know.' If you used any assumptions to arrive at your answer, please clearly state what assumptions are made."

Task-specific prompts aur XML tags

Ab tak ke prompt templates bahut generic ya task-agnostic hain. Agar aapko pata hai ki users kis nature ki queries poochhenge, to aap prompts ko zyada specific aur effective banane ke liye tailor kar sakte hain. Example ke liye, agar aapko pata hai ki task question answering hai, to aapka prompt template simplify ho sakta hai: "Answer the question {query}, given the context {retrieved_results}." Ek aur example: agar aapko pata hai ki user query ek formal question nahi hai, balki ek search engine ko di jane wali search query jaisi hai, to aapka prompt template summarization ke liye tailor kiya ja sakta hai: "You are a good summarizer. Please summarize the information about {query} from the context below: {retrieved_results}." Background information provide karne se bhi LLM ka output potentially improve ho sakta hai. Example ke liye, agar aapko pata hai ki aapki RAG application ka domain science ya sports hai, to aap apna prompt ye keh kar shuru kar sakte hain ki "you are an expert in science/sports." Aakhri advice hai ki LLM ko prompt ke alag-alag parts samajhne me madad karne ke liye ek common practice hai XML tags use karke unhe delineate karna — example ke liye, query ko <query> tags me aur context ko <context> tags me rakhna.

LLMs aur prompt templates evaluate karna

Market me kai LLMs hain, aur unhe prompt karne ke kai tareeke hain. Ek natural sawaal hai: sahi LLM aur corresponding prompt template kaise pick karein? Pehla step hai evaluation queries taiyaar karna jo un types ki queries ko reflect ya mimic karein jo users RAG system ko bhej sakte hain. Agar aapke paas badi sankhya me existing user queries hain, to fantastic. Warna, queries ko synthesize karein — ek LLM ko apne data, user behavior aur potential RAG system ke baare me dusri information ke saath prompt karke. Agla step hai RAG se responses evaluate karne ke liye "critics" banana. Ek common practice hai LLM-as-a-judge. Ek baar phir, hum LLMs ki instruction-following capability leverage karte hain taaki unhe evaluators ke roop me configure kiya ja sake jo responses ke alag-alag aspects judge karte hain. Usually do common aspects hote hain: relevance — kya response query ka jawab deta hai? aur faithfulness — kya response retrieved documents se well-supported hai? Hum generation aur evaluation dono ke liye same LLM use kar sakte hain. LLMs ki instruction-following capability ki wajah se ek LLM ko alag-alag tasks perform karne ke liye configure kiya ja sakta hai.

LLM-as-a-judge ki drawbacks, aur alternatives

LLM-as-a-judge ki kai drawbacks hain. Pehle, woh slow aur expensive ho sakta hai, kyunki woh expensive LLMs use karta hai. Dusre, woh hamesha accurate nahi bhi ho sakta. LLMs hallucinate kar sakte hain — jaise ek step se dusre step tak reasoning flawed ho sakta hai, to LLM ka judgment bhi flawed ho sakta hai. Teesre, woh consistent nahi bhi ho sakta — same LLM alag-alag times par alag judgments de sakta hai. LLM-as-a-judge ka ek alternative hai dedicated natural language generation (NLG) evaluation models, jo generally LLMs se bahut chhote hote hain. LLM generation ke specific aspects evaluate karne ke liye fine-tune kiye gaye, ye models LLM-as-a-judge se bahut faster, cheaper aur zyada robust hote hain. Example ke liye, ek mashhoor faithfulness-judging model hai jo August 2024 me debut ke baad August 2025 tak 5 million se zyada baar download hua tha. Ek dusra hallucination-judging model bhi hai. Evaluation ka aakhri, lekin golden, form hai human evaluation. Human evaluators LLM responses ke sabse accurate aur nuanced assessments provide kar sakte hain — context, intent aur subtlety ko dhyaan me rakhte hue, jo automated systems miss kar sakte hain. Lekin human evaluation sabse resource-intensive aur time-consuming method bhi hai. Ye aksar automated evaluations ke baad final, small-scale check ke roop me use hoti hai. LLMs aur prompt templates evaluate karne ke liye, simply evaluation queries ko RAG system ko bhejo aur responses collect karo. Phir, established critics ka use karke responses ki quality assess karo. Agar aapke evaluation criteria multifaceted hain, to alag-alag aspects ko account karne ke liye ek weighted scoring system use karne par consider karo. Aakhir me, bas LLM aur prompt template ka woh combination pick karo jo aapke evaluation criteria ke according best performance deta hai.

Code example — Anthropic Claude se responses generate karna

Book me ek straightforward demo hai jisme LLMs aur prompt templates ka use karke user queries aur context ke basis par responses generate kiye jate hain. Context ke roop me evaluation wale section ka asal text use kiya gaya hai, aur ek leading model ko teen queries present ki jati hain: pehli — agar budget ya time ki parwah na ho, to RAG system judge karne ka sabse accurate tareeka kya hai? dusri — log RAG system ko commonly kin aspects par judge karte hain? teesri — RAG system evaluate karne ke kitne tareeke hain, sirf method names. Prompt template kuch is tarah hai: "You are a good reader. Answer the query based on the context provided. Give me a short answer. Query: {query}. Context: {context}." Phir model ko Python API ke through request ki jati hai. Pehli query par response aata hai ki human evaluation sabse accurate tareeka hai, jab budget aur time constraints nahi hain — context explicitly kehta hai ki human evaluators sabse accurate aur nuanced assessments provide kar sakte hain, aur use "golden evaluation" describe karta hai. Dusri query par response aata hai ki log commonly do main aspects par judge karte hain — relevance (kya response asal me query ka jawab deta hai) aur faithfulness (kya response retrieved documents se well supported hai) — aur ye evaluations LLM-as-a-judge, dedicated NLG evaluation models, ya human evaluation se perform ki ja sakti hain. Teesri query par response aata hai ki RAG systems evaluate karne ke 3 tareeke hain — LLM-as-a-judge, NLG evaluation models, aur human evaluation. Teeno test queries me model ke responses relevant aur context ke prati faithful hain — jo dikhata hai ki simple prompt template effective hai.

Yaad rakho: Generation step me embeddings nahi, original text chunks + original user query jati hai. Prompt me query ko context se pehle rakho, "I don't know" kehne ki permission do, XML tags se parts alag karo — aur LLM/prompt chunne se pehle relevance aur faithfulness par evaluate karo, sirf feel se nahi.
generative-llms.ipynb — Generative LLMs for RAG — GitHub: ofermend/hands-on-rag, chapter2/generative-llms.ipynb (https://github.com/ofermend/hands-on-rag/blob/main/chapter2/generative-llms.ipynb)
# Save ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in a .env file

import dotenv
dotenv.load_dotenv()

import anthropic


query = "If I don't care about budget or time, what's the most accurate way to judge the RAG system?"

context = """
The next step is to build the critics for evaluating the responses from RAG. A common practice is called **LLM-as-a-judge**. 
Once again, we leverage the instruction following capability of LLMs to configure them into evaluators that judge different aspects of the responses. 

There are usually two common aspects: 
**relevance** -- does the response answer the query? and 
**faithfulness** -- is the response well supported by the retrieved documents? 

LLM-as-a-judge has several drawbacks. 
First, it maybe slow and expensive because it uses expensive LLMs. 
Second, it may not always be accurate. LLMs can hallucinate, e.g., the reasoning from one step to another may be flawed. 

An alternative to LLM-as-a-judge is dedicated **NLG (natural language generation) evaluation models** which are generally much smaller than an LLM. 
Finetuned to evaluate specific aspects of LLM generation, these models are much faster, cheaper, and more robust than LLM-as-a-judge. 
For example, Vectara's HHEM is a time-tested model to judge faithfulness. 
It has been downloaded more than 5 million times between August 2024 (when it debut) and August 2025. 

The last, but golden evaluation is **human evaluation**. 
Human evaluators can provide the most accurate and nuanced assessments of LLM responses, taking into account context, intent, and subtlety that automated systems may miss.
However, human evaluation is also the most resource-intensive and time-consuming method. 
It is often used as a final, small-scale check after automated evaluations have been performed.
"""

prompt_template= """
You are a good reader. Answer the query based on the context provided. Give me a short answer. 

Query: {query}
Context: {context}

"""

model_name = 'claude-sonnet-4-5'
response = anthropic.Anthropic().messages.create(
    model=model_name,
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": prompt_template.format(query=query, context=context)}
    ]
)
print (response.content[0].text)

# A different query
query = "What are the common aspects that people judge the RAG system on?"

response = anthropic.Anthropic().messages.create(
    model=model_name,
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": prompt_template.format(query=query, context=context)}
    ]
)
print (response.content[0].text)

# Yet another different query
query = "How many ways to evaluate the RAG system? Just method names."

response = anthropic.Anthropic().messages.create(
    model=model_name,
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": prompt_template.format(query=query, context=context)}
    ]
)
print (response.content[0].text)

03Chapter 3 · Scaling Your RAG Stack

Scaling Your RAG Stack — RAG at scale challenges

Chapter 2 me aapne RAG stack ke basic components dekhe — parsing, chunking, embedding, vector search aur LLM se generation. Is knowledge se aap chhote ya medium datasets par end-to-end RAG application bana sakte hain jo kaafi achha kaam karegi. Lekin jab application enterprise scale par pahunchti hai, to kahani badal jati hai. Is chapter me hum un advanced techniques ko dekhte hain jo aapke RAG stack ko bina latency ya response quality khoye enterprise scale tak le jati hain — data ingestion, advanced retrieval, guardrails aur hallucination handling. Security aur data privacy scale par aur bhi important ho jati hai, aur woh Chapter 4 me detail me aati hai. Chapter ke end me ek aisi cheez par baat hogi jise aksar ignore kar diya jata hai lekin jo utni hi critical hai — ek great user experience, taaki aapka frontend aapke backend jitna hi achha ho.

Scale ka matlab sirf "zyada documents" nahi hai

Jab aapki RAG application grow karti hai, to cheezein jaldi complex ho jati hain. Aapko zyada volume ke documents aur queries handle karne padte hain, multiple document formats aate hain, high-quality responses maintain karne ke liye advanced retrieval mechanisms chahiye hote hain, hallucination mitigation aur guardrails lagane padte hain — aur ye sab ek saath. Scale ke teen dimensions ko samajhna zaroori hai: data ka volume, documents ki complexity aur query load. In teeno ko samajhne ke baad hi aap RAG ke har component par scale ka asar dekh sakte hain, ingestion se shuru karke.

Volume and complexity of documents

Scale-up ka sabse basic component hai documents ki sankhya badhana. Ek document ya dus documents ke liye RAG stack banana relatively easy hai, lekin jab hundreds of thousands ya millions of documents handle karne padte hain, to indexing aur fast (low-latency) retrieval support karna bilkul trivial nahi rehta. Document ka size bhi challenge ban jata hai — chhote documents parse aur chunk karna easy hai, lekin kuch PDF files bahut badi hoti hain. Book me ek example hai ek 5,000 pages wale document ka — use parse karna kaafi slow ho sakta hai aur usse bahut zyada chunks ban jate hain. Scale ka matlab bade query volume se bhi ho sakta hai: jaise-jaise queries per second (QPS) badhti hai, low latency maintain karne ke liye RAG stack ke saare parts me horizontal scaling, rate limiting aur caching chahiye hoti hai.

Jaise-jaise documents aur chunks ki sankhya badhti hai, ek aur problem ubharti hai: retrieval accuracy degrade ho sakti hai. Reason simple hai — chunks bahut zyada ho jate hain, aur top-k results me sabse relevant chunks retrieve karna significantly mushkil ho jata hai, jisse noise signal ko overwhelm karne ka risk badh jata hai. Simple vector similarity search best passages ko consistently sahi rank karne me struggle kar sakti hai, aur yahin better retrieval techniques — jaise hybrid search aur reranking — zaroori ho jati hain, jinhe aap is chapter me aage "Advanced Retrieval" me dekhenge.

Index freshness — data purana ho gaya to jawab bhi purana

Scalable RAG maintenance aur data freshness ke aas-paas significant challenges laata hai. Dynamic data wale environments me, jahan documents constantly add, update ya delete hote rehte hain, RAG system ki knowledge base ko current rakhna crucial hai. Millions of documents ki full re-indexing prohibitively slow aur expensive ho sakti hai. Isliye aapko ek efficient incremental update pipeline implement karni padti hai — changes detect karne, sirf affected documents ya chunks ko selectively re-embed aur re-index karne, aur deletions ko gracefully handle karne ki strategies ke saath. Data freshness ko address na karne se RAG system stale ya inaccurate information dene lagta hai, jo user trust ko undermine karta hai. Is topic par detail me "Advanced Data Ingestion" me baat hogi.

Cost management and optimization — ek worked example

Scale par sabse critical component hai cost. Millions of documents aur high query volumes wala RAG system chalane me substantial kharcha aata hai — storage (raw data, chunked text, vector indices), compute (embedding generation, indexing processes, query-time retrieval computation, LLM inference) aur third-party models ya services ke API usage fees. Book ek typical analysis deta hai: maan lo ek customer support agents ke liye RAG chatbot hai jo 2 million documents par based hai (maan lo har document 20 pages ka) aur monthly volume 150,000 queries hai.

  • Embedding cost (one-time): 2M documents × 20 pages = 40M pages. Maan lo 600 words per page aur 1.3 tokens per word, to lagbhag 800 tokens per page — total lagbhag 3.2 billion tokens. Ek bade embedding model ki rate maan lo $0.13 per 1M tokens, to initial investment lagbhag $4,160 banti hai. Regular updates aur additional documents ke liye 5–10% monthly ka budget alag se maan lo.
  • Query cost (monthly): 150K queries per month par queries ko embed karne ki cost negligible hai — asal cost LLM call me hai. RAG me input me sirf query nahi, saara context bhi jata hai, jo production-grade systems me kabhi-kabhi 2K ya 4K input tokens per query tak pahunch jata hai. Maan lo 4K input tokens aur 1K output tokens, to ye lagbhag $3,000 per month banta hai.
  • Infrastructure (monthly): vector database ke liye lagbhag $500 per month, dusre compute infrastructure ke liye $500 per month aur monitoring, observability, CI/CD aur dusre DevOps tooling ke liye $500 per month.
  • Total: $4,160 ka initial investment aur lagbhag $4,916 per month (tokens + infrastructure + additional embeddings ke liye lagbhag $416).

Costs ko control me rakhne ke liye sirf LLM API rates dekhna kaafi nahi hai — ek multilayered architectural approach chahiye, aur monitoring tools se RAG stack ke har component par cost ki visibility chahiye. Infrastructure side par isme hybrid search infrastructure ko quantization aur compression se optimize karna aata hai, taaki corpus badhne par memory usage strictly manage ho aur storage aur retrieval compute costs balloon na hon. Agar aap knowledge graphs integrate karte hain, to cost dramatically badh sakti hai, kyunki knowledge graphs ya GraphRAG build aur maintain karna bahut mehenga hota hai.

Token economics — variable kharch par control

Variable expenses curb karne ke liye token economics ko aggressively manage karna padta hai:

  • Multilevel caching: sirf final responses hi nahi, embeddings aur retrieved chunks bhi cache karo, taaki pipeline ke har stage par redundant compute se bacha ja sake.
  • Dynamic model routing: simple requests ko saste, fast models ki taraf bhejo aur premium "reasoning" models sirf complex tasks ke liye reserve rakho.
  • Component upgrades ka cost: jaise-jaise scale badhta hai, initial components (jaise embedding models ya LLMs) ko replace ya update karna pad sakta hai — example ke liye ek fast model se ek zyada accurate pro model par upgrade — jisse aksar cost badhti hai aur additional effort lagta hai.
  • Latency vs quality ka trade-off: response quality improve karne ke liye components add karte hi latency badhna bahut common hai, aur low latency wapas paane ke liye RAG stack ko phir se retune karna padta hai.

Cost control ke in aspects par Chapter 4 me aur detail me baat hogi, jahan total cost of ownership discuss hota hai.

Yaad rakho: Scale sirf "zyada data" nahi hai — ye teen cheezein ek saath hain: zyada documents aur chunks (retrieval accuracy par pressure), stale hota data (freshness pipeline ki zaroorat) aur badhta kharcha (storage + compute + tokens). In teeno ko ek saath design karo, alag-alag nahi.
SOURCESource: Hands-On RAG for Production, O'Reilly, Chapter 3 — Scaling Your RAG Stack
