07.1Chapter 7 · From RAG to AI Agents

The Agentic Loop — Tool Calling, MCP

Har AI agent ke dil me — chahe woh akela kaam kare ya multi-agent system ka hissa ho — ek continuous, iterative process chalti hai, jise agentic loop kehte hain. Is loop ko samajhna hi agent ko debug karne ki chaabi hai, kyunki loop iterative hai: ek step me failure agle cycle ki observation ko bigaad deta hai, aur bina proper instrumentation ke root cause dhoondhna mushkil ho jata hai.

Loop ke teen stages

  • 1. Observation: Loop shuru hota hai agent ke apni current state aur environment ke baare me information gather karne se. Pehla input user ki query ho sakti hai ("mere aas-paas best-rated Italian restaurants dhoondho"), aur baad ke cycles me pichhle action ka output (jaise web search tool call ke results).
  • 2. Reasoning and planning: Latest information haath me aane par agent ka LLM brain reasoning karta hai. Ye poora context process karta hai — initial goal, pichhle steps ki memory, aur nayi observation — progress assess karta hai aur agla logical step decide karta hai. Phir LLM plan banata hai aur decide karta hai ki goal achieve karne ke liye kaunse tools call karne hain, kin arguments ke saath.
  • 3. Action: Orchestration layer plan ko execute karta hai — LLM ke tool call requests ko interpret karke un tools ko diye gaye arguments ke saath chalata hai, phir results wapas LLM ko bhejta hai. Tools retrieval ya RAG pipeline call kar sakte hain, relational database query kar sakte hain, ya internal ya external API call kar sakte hain.

Loop complete hone ke baad agent tool calls ke results observe karta hai, aur ye cycle tab tak repeat hota hai jab tak reasoning LLM ye determine na kar le ki overall goal successfully achieve ho gaya hai.

Unstructured data ke saath: retrieval tool ya RAG tool?

Agentic RAG me documents se information nikalte waqt do designs possible hain. Retrieval tool relevant documents ya chunks return karta hai aur reasoning aur answer synthesis agent par chhod deta hai — isse agent ko zyada control aur transparency milti hai, jo complex ya exploratory workflows ke liye behtar hai. RAG tool khud retrieval aur response generation karke grounded answer (aksar citations ke saath) return karta hai — isse grounding logic centralize hoti hai aur zyada consistent answers milte hain, kam agent-side orchestration ke saath. Dono valid hain, aur koi bhi inherently zyada "agentic" nahi hai. Choice is baat par depend karti hai ki responsibility agent aur tool ke beech kaise split karni hai — aur agentic systems aksar product goals ke hisaab se dono approaches ko mix bhi karte hain.

Tool calling — LLM ko active participant banana

Tool calling (function calling ke naam se bhi jaana jata hai) LLMs ki woh recent capability hai jo LLM ko agentic workflow me active participant bana deti hai. 2023 ke shuru me ek influential paper aaya jisne dikhaya ki language model khud seekh sakta hai ki kaunsi API call karni hai, kab karni hai, kaunse parameters use karne hain, aur results ko output me kaise incorporate karna hai. Usi saal ReAct framework aaya — LLM reasoning aur action steps ko interleave karta hai: query ka jawab dene ke liye kya chahiye, is par thought generate karo, action karo (jaise search engine query karna), result observe karo, aur us observation se agla thought aur action inform karo. Practical adoption tab aayi jab commercial LLMs ne function calling ko apne API me integrate kiya — 2023 ke mid me OpenAI ka function calling ek landmark moment tha.

Tool calling developers ko ek structured tareeka deta hai functions ko model ko describe karne ka, aur model apne response me ek JSON object generate karta hai jisme zaroori arguments hote hain. Example: get_weather naam ka tool define karo — description "Get current temperature for provided coordinates in Celsius", parameters latitude aur longitude (dono number, dono required). User poochhe "Oakland me aaj mausam kaisa hai?" to model jawab deta hai: get_weather call karo, arguments latitude 37.8044, longitude -122.2711 ke saath — jo exactly Oakland ki location hai. Orchestration layer ab is tool call ko execute karta hai (asli get_weather function ko un arguments ke saath call karke), actual temperature leta hai, aur use wapas LLM ko deta hai, jo us information se final response banata hai.

Shuru me tool calling aksar ek user query (ya ek turn) par ek hi tool call tak limited thi. Lekin complex interactions ke liye parallel tool calling aayi — LLM ek hi turn me multiple alag tools call kar sakta hai. Example: ek company ka 2021, 2022 aur 2023 ka revenue compare karna ho to agent get_revenue(year, ticker) ko teen baar parallel me call kar sakta hai, alag year values ke saath, kyunki ye calls ek dusre se independent hain. Aaj lagbhag har modern LLM tool calling support karta hai, aur iski accuracy tezi se improve ho rahi hai.

Lekin tool calling perfect nahi hai — production me iske liye careful tool design chahiye. Sabse bada failure mode hai incorrect tool use: LLM galat tool select karta hai ya galat argument values ke saath call karta hai — khaas taur par jab tool names ya descriptions overlap karte hon ya ambiguous hon. Mitigation ke liye output validation karo (tool names aur arguments valid hain ya nahi), retry logic lagao (tool call ke error messages ko wapas LLM ko feed karo), aur "max turns" jaise execution constraints lagao taaki uncontrolled cost roki ja sake. Reliability model ki choice par bhi depend karti hai — same family me version upgrade ya provider switch karne se identical tool descriptions alag outcomes trigger kar sakti hain. Production me tool calls ko unpredictable inputs ki tarah treat karo jinhe sanitize karna padta hai, aur woh LLMs chuno jinhe tumne apne specific toolset par accuracy ke liye test kiya ho. Aur tool design me ek basic rule yaad rakho: generic naam jaise data_lookup "tool confusion" paida karta hai — model use irrelevant queries ke liye bhi invoke kar sakta hai. Iske bajaye semantic naam do jo intent signal kare, precisely typed arguments do, aur description me tool ka scope aur boundaries dono specify karo.

Model Context Protocol (MCP) — tools ke liye universal interface

Jab specialized tools ka explosion hua, to ek nayi problem dikhi: AI agents ke unse interact karne ka koi unified tareeka nahi tha. Is fragmentation ka jawab hai MCP — ek open protocol jo standardize karta hai ki LLMs tools invoke kaise karein aur data access kaise karein, aur AI agent ko tools ki specific implementation details se decouple kar deta hai. Is standardization se koi bhi data source ya API ek universal interface ke through "agent-ready" ban sakta hai. Protocol teen core primitives define karta hai:

  • Tools (dynamic interaction): Executable functions jinhe agent discover aur call kar sakta hai. Ye actions karne ke liye bhi use hote hain (jaise email bhejna) aur dynamic tareeke se data padhne ka primary tareeka bhi hain (jaise database query karna ya live API response fetch karna).
  • Resources (context and state): Ye protocol ki "data layer" hain, URIs se identify hote hain (jaise file:// ya postgres://), aur contextual information share karne ka standardized tareeka dete hain. Ye aksar lengthy data ya state ke liye use hote hain jo ek single tool response se nahi bheja jana chahiye. Example: ek tool complex analysis karke Resource ka URI return karta hai, aur LLM full results ko alag se "padh" sakta hai aur context ko time ke saath maintain rakh sakta hai.
  • Prompts (interaction templates): Predefined, reusable instruction templates jo kisi specific task ko accomplish karne ke best practices encode karte hain. Ye agent ko intent, constraints aur expected behavior dekar structured guidance dete hain, taaki interactions consistent aur high-quality hon. Ye parameterized ho sakte hain aur tools ya resources ko reference kar sakte hain, lekin khud logic execute nahi karte — ye common workflows (jaise data analysis ya summarization) ke liye well-formed starting points hain.

MCP architecture — host, client, server

MCP architecture classic client–server model par hai, jo AI application ki concerns ko tool provider se cleanly separate karta hai:

  • MCP host: Woh AI application ya environment jahan AI agent operate karta hai — wahi system jise end user directly interact karta hai. Ye VSCode jaise IDE (GitHub Copilot ke saath), Claude Code Desktop jaise conversational interface, ya custom-built agentic framework ho sakta hai.
  • MCP client: Host ke andar rehne wala component jo agent ke tool use karne ke intent ko structured request me translate karke appropriate MCP server ko bhejta hai. Ye protocol ke mechanics handle karta hai — requests aur response streams parse karna, interaction ka state manage karna.
  • MCP server: Typically ek lightweight service jo MCP client aur ek ya zyada tools ke beech intermediary ka kaam karta hai — ek "adapter" ki tarah. Ye kisi bhi client se standardized requests leta hai aur unhe underlying system ke liye specific commands ya API calls me translate karta hai. Example: Text2SQL ke liye MCP server agent se aayi natural language request ko valid SQL query me badal kar execute karta hai aur results ko standardized MCP format me wapas bhejta hai.

Ek important detail: MCP intentionally authentication, authorization aur key management ko apne scope se bahar chhodta hai — ye concerns host aur server ki implementation par chhodi gayi hain, isliye enterprise deployment me inhe alag se design karna padta hai.

MCP in enterprise — business value kahan hai

MCP sirf integration protocol nahi hai; enterprise deployments me ye secure aur scalable agentic AI ka foundational enabler hai:

  • Agent governance and security: MCP ek critical mediation layer hai jo AI applications ko sensitive tools aur data tak arbitrary ya unmanaged access se rokta hai. Ye AI agent aur enterprise systems ke beech ek "trust boundary" establish karke governed, secure aur auditable connectivity ke standardized rules define karta hai. Enterprise role-based access controls aur fine-grained permissions enforce karke ye ensure karta hai ki agents sirf authorized parameters ke andar operate karein.
  • Scalability and cost efficiency: Cloud infrastructure concepts (jaise Kubernetes-hosted control planes) se inspiration lekar, ek single shared MCP server multiple agentic applications ke saare agent requests manage kar sakta hai — har interaction ke liye dedicated infrastructure ki zaroorat khatm ho jati hai. Agents aur services ka decoupling dono components ko independently scale karne deta hai.
  • Maintainability and reusability: MCP organization ke scattered internal data systems ko "AI-ready" tools ki coherent, reusable library me transform kar deta hai. Legacy systems — jaise mainframes aur internal databases — ko MCP server me "wrap" karke AI agents ke liye securely accessible banaya ja sakta hai, bina expensive aur disruptive system overhauls ke.

Lekin developer ko standardization ke long-term benefits ko direct integration ki immediate simplicity se weigh karna chahiye. Ek localized application ke liye — jaise ek single internal product jo narrow, static set of tools use karta ho — MCP server ki added layer unnecessary overhead ho sakti hai; rapid prototyping aur deployment ke liye direct API coupling aksar zyada efficient hoti hai. MCP me investment tab essential hoti hai jab isolated use cases se shared enterprise AI ecosystem ki taraf move karna ho — jahan multiple independent agents ko tools ki common library access karni ho, ya sensitive legacy data ko unified security aur auditing wrapper chahiye ho.

Agent-to-agent communication (A2A) — horizontal layer

MCP agent ko tools aur data tak governed access deta hai — ye communication ki "vertical" stack hai. Agent2Agent (A2A) complementary "horizontal" layer hai: ek open protocol jo agents ko ek dusre se communicate aur coordinate karne deta hai, aur MCP ki core capabilities ko directly augment karta hai. Example: ek "project manager" agent high-level goal lekar A2A se subtasks ek "database querying" agent aur ek "report-writing" agent ko delegate kar sakta hai. Isse sirf tools reusable nahi hote — specialized agents khud modular, reusable components ban jate hain bade intelligent system me.

A2A ka key concept hai Agent Card — har AI agent ke liye ek digital profile jo uski specific skills, perform kar sakne wale tasks ke types, aur process kar sakne wale data ko detail me batata hai. Jab ek agent ko madad chahiye hoti hai, to woh Agent Cards consult karke requisite capabilities wala dusra agent search aur identify kar sakta hai. Suitable agent milne par woh secure aur structured dialogue initiate karke tasks delegate kar sakta hai, data share kar sakta hai, aur progress monitor kar sakta hai. A2A ek common language banakar sophisticated aur comprehensive AI solutions ka development facilitate karta hai, aur ensure karta hai ki alag vendors ke specialized agents ek unified team ki tarah kaam kar sakein. Protocol ki technical specifications a2a.cx par available hain.

Yaad rakho: Loop ke teen stages — observe, reason, act — baar-baar repeat hote hain jab tak goal poora na ho. Tool calling me tool ka naam, typed arguments aur description hi model ki samajh hai — inhe carefully likho. MCP tools ko standardize karta hai (vertical), A2A agents ko connect karta hai (horizontal) — dono milkar multi-agent enterprise systems possible banate hain.
tool-calling.ipynb — Tool Calling with LLMs — GitHub: ofermend/hands-on-rag, chapter7/tool-calling.ipynb (https://github.com/ofermend/hands-on-rag/blob/main/chapter7/tool-calling.ipynb)
from openai import OpenAI

weather_tool = {
    "type": "function",
    "name": "get_weather",
    "description": "Get current temperature for provided coordinates in Celsius.",
    "parameters": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "latitude": { "type": "number" },
            "longitude": { "type": "number" }
        },
        "required": ["latitude", "longitude"],
        "additionalProperties": False
    },
}

#def get_weather(latitude: float, longitude: float):
    # get the weather somehow

client = OpenAI()
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather like in Oakland today?"}
    ],
    functions=[weather_tool],
    function_call={"name": "get_weather"}
)

response.choices[0].message.function_call
vectara-agent.ipynb — RAG Agent with Vectara — GitHub: ofermend/hands-on-rag, chapter7/vectara-agent.ipynb (https://github.com/ofermend/hands-on-rag/blob/main/chapter7/vectara-agent.ipynb)
import json
import requests
import os

VECTARA_CORPUS_KEY = "hands-on-rag"
VECTARA_API_KEY = os.getenv('VECTARA_API_KEY')

url = f"https://api.vectara.io/v2/corpora/{VECTARA_CORPUS_KEY}/upload_file"

payload={}
files=[
  ('file',('gpt-2-paper',open('language_models_are_unsupervised_multitask_learners.pdf','rb'),'application/octet-stream'))
]
headers = {
  'Accept': 'application/json',
  'x-api-key': VECTARA_API_KEY
}

response = requests.request("POST", url, headers=headers, data=payload, files=files)
res = response.json()
print(response.status_code)

tool_configurations = {
    "rag_search": {
        "type": "corpora_search",
        "query_configuration": {
            "search": {
                "limit": 50,
                "corpora": [
                    {
                        "corpus_key": VECTARA_CORPUS_KEY,
                        "lexical_interpolation": 0.01,
                    }
                ],
                "context_configuration": {
                    "sentences_before": 2,
                    "sentences_after": 2
                },
                "reranker": {
                    "type": "customer_reranker",
                    "reranker_name": "Rerank_Multilingual_v1",
                    "cutoff": 0.3
                }
            },
        }
    },
}

agent_key = "my-agent"

create_agent_obj = {
    "key": agent_key,
    "name": "GPT-2 Agent",
    "description": "This agent handles queries and conversations related to the original GPT-2 paper about transformers.", 
    "tool_configurations": tool_configurations,
    "model": {
        "name": 'gpt-4o'
    },
    "first_step": {
        "type": "conversational",
        "instructions": [
            {
                "type": "inline",
                "name": "A Simple agent to ask questions about GPT-2 paper",
                "template": """
                    You are a chatbot that can answer questions about the GPT-2 paper.
                    Only answer questions related to GPT-2 and the original paper, and based on information provided by the tools.
                    Always respond to the user in English.
                """
            }
        ],
        "output_parser": {
            "type": "default"
        }
    }
}

headers = {
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "Accept": "application/json",
    "x-api-key": VECTARA_API_KEY
}

# Always delete existing agent first (this also deletes all its sessions)
delete_url = f"https://api.vectara.io/v2/agents/{agent_key}"
delete_response = requests.delete(delete_url, headers=headers)
if delete_response.status_code == 204:
    print(f"Deleted existing agent '{agent_key}'")
elif delete_response.status_code == 404:
    print(f"Agent '{agent_key}' does not exist, creating new one")
else:
    print(f"Delete returned: {delete_response.status_code}")

# Create the agent
url = "https://api.vectara.io/v2/agents"
response = requests.post(url, json=create_agent_obj, headers=headers)
print(f"Create agent status: {response.status_code}")
if response.status_code != 201:
    print(response.text)

import time

# Use unique session key and name to avoid conflicts with orphaned sessions
timestamp = int(time.time())
session_key = f"session-{timestamp}"
session_name = f"GPT-2 session {timestamp}"
print(f"Using session: key={session_key}, name={session_name}")

headers = {
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
    'Accept': 'application/json',
    'x-api-key': VECTARA_API_KEY,
}

# Create the session
url = f"https://api.vectara.io/v2/agents/{agent_key}/sessions"
payload = {
    "key": session_key,
    "name": session_name,
    "description": "Help users with questions about GPT-2",
    "enabled": True
}

response = requests.post(url, headers=headers, json=payload)
print(f"Create session status: {response.status_code}")
if response.status_code != 201:
    print(response.text)

url = f"https://api.vectara.io/v2/agents/{agent_key}/sessions/{session_key}/events"
query = "What is GPT-2?"

payload = {
    "type": "input_message",
    "messages": [
        {
            "type": "text",
            "content": query,
        }
    ],
    "stream_response": False
}
headers = {
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
    'Accept': 'application/json',
    'x-api-key': VECTARA_API_KEY,
}

response = requests.post(url, headers=headers, json=payload)
print(f"Events status: {response.status_code}")

res = response.json()
if 'events' in res:
    print(res['events'][-1])
else:
    print(f"Error: {res}")

if 'events' in res:

← Previous07 · From RAG to AI Agents — What Is an AI Agent?→ Next07.2 · Hands-On with Agentic AI Frameworks
07.2Chapter 7 · From RAG to AI Agents

Hands-On with Agentic AI Frameworks

Agent concepts samajhne ke baad asli seekh haath se banane me hai. Is chapter me chaar alag frameworks se agents banaye gaye hain — LangChain se chatbot, LlamaIndex se document generation agent, Vectara se managed agent, aur CrewAI se multi-agent system. Har example ek alag pattern dikhata hai, aur saath me ye bhi dikhata hai ki demo se production tak jaane ke liye kya-kya add karna padta hai.

AI chatbots using LangChain — ReAct agent kaam me

LangChain example me ek ReAct agent banaya gaya hai jo ek RAG tool (rag_gpt_tool) use karta hai. Tool ka kaam hai ek research paper ke content par based sawalon ka jawab dena — paper hai "Language Models Are Unsupervised Multitask Learners", jo GPT-2 ko introduce karta hai. Agent ko ek complex sawal diya jata hai: GPT-2 ka size kya hai aur woh size uski performance ko kaise influence karta hai?

ReAct algorithm is complex sawal ko do subquestions me tod deta hai: pehla, GPT-2 ka size weights ki sankhya ke hisaab se kya hai; dusra, size uski performance ko kaise affect karta hai. Phir agent rag_gpt_tool ko do baar call karta hai — ek baar har subquestion ke saath. Har call par ReAct ek observation leta hai, aur aakhir me agent dono observations se final answer compile karta hai. Is example se do cheezein saaf dikhti hain: pehli, agent sawal ko decompose karke har hisse ke liye separately retrieve karta hai (single retrieval se zyada precise); dusri, reasoning aur action ka interleaving hi ReAct ki taakat hai — thought, action, observation, phir agla thought.

Ye LangChain ka bahut simple use case hai — framework se aur bhi kai tarah ke agentic workflows implement kiye ja sakte hain. Lekin production me is simple demo ko robust banane ke liye kai mechanisms add karne padte hain: timeouts aur retry policies, saare tool calls ki extensive tracing aur logging (debugging aur auditability ke liye), aur agent execution ki monitoring taaki tool calls me infinite loops se bacha ja sake. Demo me loop theek lagta hai; production me loop hi sabse bada risk hai.

Document generation agent with LlamaIndex — teen tools, ek plan

LlamaIndex example zyada advanced hai: ek agent jo teen tools use karta hai — Tavily service se web search tool, arbitrary mathematical expressions compute karne wala calc tool, aur ek RAG tool jo GPT-2 wale paper ke content par based generated responses deta hai. Tavily aur Exa modern category ke tools hain jinhe agentic search services kehte hain: traditional search engines humans ke liye links ki list dete hain, jabki ye services LLMs aur autonomous agents ke liye internet ko real time me "padhne" ke liye bani hain — web content ko retrieve karke clean aur structure karke Markdown ya JSON jaise machine-readable formats me deti hain.

Agent FunctionAgent class se define hota hai, aur uska LLM brain Claude Sonnet 4.5 hai. Har tool FunctionTool class se define hota hai — jaise web search tool ek async function hai jo Tavily client se advanced search depth par query karta hai aur results ko string ke roop me return karta hai, saath me ek clear name aur description ("Search the web for fresh information and return relevant results with links"). Saare tools banne ke baad agent ko ek system_prompt diya jata hai jo uska behavior define karta hai: "You are a research & planning assistant. Use tools when helpful. Prefer rag_tool for questions about GPT-2. When using web_search, summarize concisely and include source links. Show brief, actionable plans." System prompt aksar customize kiya jata hai taaki agent ke specific behavior traits define ho sakein.

Agent ko phir ek practical query di jati hai: Saturday ko Santa Cruz ka day trip plan karna — 2–3 must-do activities (links ke saath), do adults ke liye total ticket costs estimate karna, aur 6-hour itinerary suggest karna. Agent run karte waqt do important cheezein dikhti hain: pehli, agent ko sirf query nahi, Context bhi diya jata hai — wahi jagah jahan query aur response history automatically store hoti hai; dusri, execution ko event stream ke roop me observe kiya ja sakta hai — AgentInput (agent ko kya input mila), AgentStream (token-level model output), ToolCall (kaunsa tool, kin arguments ke saath), ToolCallResult (tool ne kya return kiya), aur AgentOutput (final response). Agent pehle web search se activities aur ticket prices dhoondhta hai, phir calculator tool se total cost compute karta hai, aur aakhir me tight 6-hour itinerary ke saath final answer deta hai. Ye event stream hi woh instrumentation hai jo debugging aur observability ke liye chahiye hoti hai — bina iske agent ek black box rehta hai.

Building an agent with Vectara — managed platform approach

Vectara example ek alag philosophy dikhata hai: agent ko khud orchestrate karne ke bajaye ek managed platform par banana. Vectara me agent ek corpus (jaise "hands-on-rag" naam ka corpus) ke upar define hota hai, API key se authenticate hota hai, aur platform khud retrieval, generation aur observability ka heavy lifting karta hai. Developer ka kaam agent ki configuration aur behavior define karna rehta hai — kaunsa corpus use karna hai, kaunse tools available hain, aur agent ko kaise respond karna hai.

Is approach ka fayda ye hai ki production concerns — jaise tracing, evaluation datasets, aur monitoring — platform ke andar hi built-in milte hain, alag se assemble nahi karne padte. Trade-off ye hai ki control kam milta hai: orchestration logic platform ke andar hoti hai, aur customization uski capabilities tak limited rehti hai. Teams ke liye jo jaldi production me jaana chahti hain aur apna orchestration framework maintain nahi karna chahti, managed approach aksar sahi starting point hota hai; jo teams ko fine-grained control chahiye, woh LangChain ya LlamaIndex jaise frameworks prefer karti hain.

Multi-agent system with CrewAI — crew, roles, tasks

CrewAI example multi-agent pattern ko concrete banata hai. Ek "crew" me har agent ki distinct role, backstory aur capabilities ya tools hote hain, aur woh collectively ek user goal address karte hain — goal ko specific tasks me todkar, har task appropriate agent ko assign karke. Agents collaboratively kaam karte hain — sequentially ya parallel, defined process ke hisaab se — jahan ek agent ka output aksar agle agent ka input hota hai. Isse multistep problems tackle hote hain, har agent ki specialized expertise leverage karke, aur final result single agent se zyada comprehensive aur nuanced hota hai.

Example me do agents define kiye gaye hain: pehla Senior Market Research Analyst, jiska goal AI field me groundbreaking aur emerging trends dhoondhna hai — backstory me use expert market research analyst bataya gaya hai jo technological shifts ko scan karta hai; dusra Technology Content Strategist, jiska goal research findings par based compelling blog post craft karna hai — backstory me use complex topics ko engaging articles me simplify karne wala strategist bataya gaya hai. Dono ke paas verbose=True aur allow_delegation=False set hai. Phir do tasks define hote hain: research task — current year ke AI aur LLM ke top 3 most significant emerging trends identify aur analyze karo, har trend ke liye title, concise summary, potential market impact, aur key companies ya research labs ke saath detailed report banao; aur writing task — us report par based blog post likho. Research agent pehle kaam karta hai, phir writer agent us report ko lekar blog post likhta hai — output ke pehle paragraphs me hi dikhta hai ki kaise communication, creativity aur transformation jaise themes ko research se article me badla gaya hai.

Multi-agent kyun behtar ho sakta hai — teen reasons

CrewAI example ke baad book teen reasons deti hai ki multi-agent systems kabhi-kabhi single agent se behtar perform karte hain:

  • The tool bottleneck: Ek single agent ke paas jab bahut zyada tools hote hain, to "tool dilution" hoti hai — galat tool chunne ya hallucinate karne ki probability badh jati hai. Multi-agent systems is failure mode ko minimize karte hain kyunki har agent ko sirf uski specific role ke liye relevant, tightly scoped set of tools milta hai.
  • Cognitive precision: "Lost in the middle" phenomenon par research dikhati hai ki LLM ki performance degrade hoti hai jab context badhta hai. Complex problem ko chhote agent-led tasks me todne se har subagent ko chhota context chahiye hota hai, jisse har ek ka focus zyada hota hai aur overall accuracy behtar hoti hai.
  • Cost efficiency: Ye counterintuitive lag sakta hai — zyada agents ka matlab zyada calls — lekin jab har agent chhote, focused context par kaam karta hai aur galat tool calls ya retries kam hote hain, to total cost aur latency dono control me reh sakte hain. Specialization se waste kam hota hai.

Lekin ye benefits free nahi hain — jaisa pehle section me dekha, multi-agent ka complexity tax (latency, token cost, debugging mushkil) hamesha hisaab me rakhna chahiye. Framework chaahe koi bhi ho — LangChain, LlamaIndex, Vectara ya CrewAI — production readiness framework se nahi, uske aas-paas ki engineering se aati hai: timeouts, retries, tracing, loop monitoring, aur evaluation.

Yaad rakho: Framework sirf orchestration deta hai — reliability tumhe khud banani padti hai. Har tool call trace karo, har loop par max-turns cap lagao, aur demo ko production samajhne ki galti mat karo. Multi-agent tabhi chuno jab specialization se accuracy ya tool confusion me real fark padta ho.
crewai-multi-agent.ipynb — Multi-Agent Systems with CrewAI — GitHub: ofermend/hands-on-rag, chapter7/crewai-multi-agent.ipynb (https://github.com/ofermend/hands-on-rag/blob/main/chapter7/crewai-multi-agent.ipynb)
import os
from crewai import Agent, Task, Crew, Process

# Agent 1: Market Research Analyst
researcher = Agent(
    role="Senior Market Research Analyst",
    goal="Find groundbreaking and emerging trends in the field of Artificial Intelligence.",
    backstory=(
        "You are an expert market research analyst with a keen eye for emerging technological trends. "
        "You continuously scan the horizon for a major technological shift, and you have a deep understanding "
        "of the AI landscape. Your goal is to identify high-potential topics that are newsworthy and relevant to a tech audience."
    ),
    verbose=True,
    allow_delegation=False,
)

# Agent 2: Technology Content Strategist
writer = Agent(
    role="Technology Content Strategist",
    goal="Craft a compelling and informative blog post based on research findings.",
    backstory=(
        "You are a renowned content strategist known for simplifying complex technological topics "
        "into engaging narratives. You take raw data and research insights and transform them into "
        "high-quality articles that resonate with both technical experts and curious beginners. "
        "Your writing style is clear, insightful, and accessible."
    ),
    verbose=True,
    allow_delegation=False,
)

# Task 1: Research AI Trends
# The 'agent' parameter assigns this task to the 'researcher' agent.
research_task = Task(
    description=(
        "Identify and analyze the top 3 most significant emerging trends in AI for the current year. "
        "Focus on trends related to large language models (LLMs), generative AI, and real-world applications. "
        "Provide a summary for each trend, highlighting its potential impact and key players."
    ),
    expected_output=(
        "A detailed report containing three emerging AI trends. Each trend section must include: "
        "1. Trend Title. "
        "2. Concise summary (2-3 sentences). "
        "3. Explanation of potential market impact. "
        "4. Key companies or research labs involved."
    ),
    agent=researcher
)

# Task 2: Write Blog Post
# This task depends on the output of 'research_task'. We define this dependency
# using the 'context' parameter. The crew will ensure 'research_task' completes
# first and its output is available to 'writer_task'.
writer_task = Task(
    description=(
        "Using the research findings provided as context, write an engaging blog post suitable for a general tech audience. "
        "The post should be approximately 500 words long. "
        "Structure the post with an introduction, sections for each of the three trends, and a concluding paragraph."
    ),
    expected_output=(
        "A well-structured and polished blog post of at least 500 words, "
        "formatted in markdown. The post must be engaging and easy to understand for non-experts."
    ),
    agent=writer,
    context=[research_task]
)

# Create the crew and define the process.
# Process.sequential means tasks will be executed one after another in the order they appear in the list.
ai_trends_crew = Crew(
    agents=[researcher, writer],
    tasks=[research_task, writer_task],
    process=Process.sequential,
    verbose=True,
)

# --- Execution ---

# Start the crew's work. The input dictionary can provide initial data for the first task.
result = ai_trends_crew.kickoff(inputs={'topic': 'AI trends'})

print("\n\n##############################")
print("## Crew Execution Finished! ##")
print("##############################\n")
print("Final Blog Post:")
print(result)
function-agent-llamaindex.ipynb — Research & Planner Agent with LlamaIndex FunctionAgent — GitHub: ofermend/hands-on-rag, chapter7/function-agent-llamaindex.ipynb (https://github.com/ofermend/hands-on-rag/blob/main/chapter7/function-agent-llamaindex.ipynb)
import os
import asyncio
from typing import Optional

from llama_index.llms.anthropic import Anthropic

from llama_index.core import Settings, SimpleDirectoryReader, VectorStoreIndex
from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import FunctionAgent, AgentWorkflow
from llama_index.core.workflow import Context
from llama_index.core.tools import FunctionTool, QueryEngineTool
from llama_index.core.callbacks import CallbackManager, LlamaDebugHandler

from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import (
    ToolCall, ToolCallResult, AgentInput, AgentOutput, AgentStream
)
from llama_index.core.workflow import Workflow

from tavily import AsyncTavilyClient

from dotenv import load_dotenv
load_dotenv()

#!pip install llama-index==0.14.14 llama-index-llms-anthropic anthropic -U --quiet

# define the LLM
model_name = "claude-sonnet-4-5"
llm = Anthropic(model=model_name)
Settings.llm = llm

# define tools: Tavily tool, calculator tool
TAVILY_API_KEY = os.getenv("TAVILY_API_KEY")

async def web_search(query: str) -> str:
    """Use the web to get up-to-date information and sources."""
    client = AsyncTavilyClient(api_key=TAVILY_API_KEY)
    result = await client.search(query, search_depth="advanced", include_raw_content=False)
    return str(result)

web_search_tool = FunctionTool.from_defaults(
    fn=web_search,
    name="web_search",
    description="Search the web for fresh information and return relevant results with links.",
)

def calc(expression: str) -> str:
    """Safely evaluate simple arithmetic expressions like '2 + 2*5'."""
    # Very minimal "safe eval" for demo purposes; expand as needed.
    allowed = set("0123456789+-*/(). %")
    if not set(expression) <= allowed:
        return "Error: Unsupported characters."
    try:
        return str(eval(expression, {"__builtins__": {}}, {}))
    except Exception as e:
        return f"Error: {e}"

calc_tool = FunctionTool.from_defaults(
    fn=calc,
    name="calculator",
    description="Evaluate basic arithmetic expressions, e.g., '12.5 * 3 - 7'.",
)

# define RAG tool
def build_rag_tool(file: str = "language_models_are_unsupervised_multitask_learners.pdf") -> Optional[QueryEngineTool]:
    try:
        docs = SimpleDirectoryReader(input_files=[file]).load_data()
        if not docs:
            return None
        index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(docs)
        qengine = index.as_query_engine(similarity_top_k=5)
        return QueryEngineTool.from_defaults(
            query_engine=qengine,
            name="gpt2-paper-tool",
            description=(
                "Answer questions from the GPT-2 paper"
            ),
            return_direct=False,
        )
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"DEBUG EXCeption {e}")
        return None

rag_tool = build_rag_tool()

tools = [web_search_tool, calc_tool, rag_tool]

# Build the agent
agent = FunctionAgent(
    tools=tools,
    llm=llm,
    system_prompt=(
        "You are a research & planning assistant. "
        "Use tools when helpful. Prefer rag_tool for questions about GPT-2 "
        "When using web_search, summarize concisely and include source links. "
        "Show brief, actionable plans."
    ),
)

ctx = Context(agent)
q1 = (
    "I'm planning a day trip to Santa Cruz this Saturday. "
    "Find 2-3 must-do activities (with links), estimate total ticket costs for two adults "
    "if needed, and suggest a 6-hour itinerary. Keep it tight."
)

# 1) Kick off the workflow (returns a handler)
handler = agent.run(user_msg=q1, ctx=ctx)

# 2) Stream events as they happen (incl. ToolCall/ToolCallResult)
async for event in handler.stream_events():
    if isinstance(event, AgentInput):
        print(f"\n🟦 AgentInput from {event.current_agent_name}:\n{event.input}")
    elif isinstance(event, AgentStream):
        # token-level model deltas
        print(event.delta, end="", flush=True)
    elif isinstance(event, ToolCall):
        print(f"\n🔧 ToolCall: {event.tool_name}  args={event}")
    elif isinstance(event, ToolCallResult):
        print(f"📥 ToolResult ({event.tool_name}): {str(event.tool_output)[:1000]}...")
    elif isinstance(event, AgentOutput):
        print(f"\n✅ Final from {event.current_agent_name}:\n{event.response.content}\n")

ctx = Context(agent)
q2 = "What are the key takeaways of the GPT-2 paper? Summarize in 5 bullets."

# 1) Kick off the workflow (returns a handler)
handler = agent.run(user_msg=q2, ctx=ctx)

# 2) Stream events as they happen (incl. ToolCall/ToolCallResult)
async for event in handler.stream_events():
    if isinstance(event, AgentInput):
        print(f"\n🟦 AgentInput from {event.current_agent_name}:\n{event.input}")
    elif isinstance(event, AgentStream):
        # token-level model deltas
        print(event.delta, end="", flush=True)
    elif isinstance(event, ToolCall):
        print(f"\n🔧 ToolCall: {event.tool_name}  args={event}")
    elif isinstance(event, ToolCallResult):
        print(f"📥 ToolResult ({event.tool_name}): {str(event.tool_output)[:1000]}...")
    elif isinstance(event, AgentOutput):
        print(f"\n✅ Final from {event.current_agent_name}:\n{event.response.content}\n")
react-agent-langchain.ipynb — ReAct Agent with LangChain — GitHub: ofermend/hands-on-rag, chapter7/react-agent-langchain.ipynb (https://github.com/ofermend/hands-on-rag/blob/main/chapter7/react-agent-langchain.ipynb)
import os
import warnings
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI, OpenAIEmbeddings
from langchain_community.document_loaders import PyPDFLoader
from langchain_community.vectorstores import FAISS
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnablePassthrough
from langchain_core.tools import tool

# Suppress deprecation warning - the suggested import location doesn't exist yet
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="create_react_agent has been moved")
from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent

# 1. Initialize the LLM and Embeddings models
llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o", temperature=0)
embeddings = OpenAIEmbeddings()

# 2. Load and Process the GPT-2 paper PDF document
loader = PyPDFLoader("language_models_are_unsupervised_multitask_learners.pdf")
docs = loader.load_and_split()

# Split the document into chunks for better processing
text_splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1000, chunk_overlap=100)
texts = text_splitter.split_documents(docs)

# 3. Create a Vector Store (Knowledge Base) using FAISS
vectorstore = FAISS.from_documents(texts, embeddings)
retriever = vectorstore.as_retriever()

# 4. Create the RAG Chain using LCEL (LangChain Expression Language)
rag_prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_template("""
Answer the question based only on the following context:
{context}

Question: {question}
""")

def format_docs(docs):
    return "\n\n".join(doc.page_content for doc in docs)

rag_chain = (
    {"context": retriever | format_docs, "question": RunnablePassthrough()}
    | rag_prompt
    | llm
    | StrOutputParser()
)

# 5. Define the RAG Tool for the Agent using @tool decorator
@tool
def rag_gpt_tool(question: str) -> str:
    """Use this tool to answer questions about the 'GPT-2' paper. 
    It can answer any question related to this topic from that original paper."""
    return rag_chain.invoke(question)

tools = [rag_gpt_tool]

# 6. Create the ReAct Agent using LangGraph
agent = create_react_agent(llm, tools)

# 7. Run the Agent with verbose output to see ReAct steps
question = "What is the size of GPT-2 in terms of number of weights? How does that influence its performance?"

print("=" * 60)
print(f"Question: {question}")
print("=" * 60)

# Stream the agent's response to see reasoning steps
for chunk in agent.stream({"messages": [("user", question)]}):
    if "agent" in chunk:
        msg = chunk["agent"]["messages"][0]
        # Check if agent is calling a tool
        if hasattr(msg, "tool_calls") and msg.tool_calls:
            for tool_call in msg.tool_calls:
                print(f"\n🔧 Action: {tool_call['name']}")
                print(f"   Input: {tool_call['args']}")
        # Print agent's reasoning/response
        if msg.content:
            print(f"\n💭 Agent: {msg.content}")
    elif "tools" in chunk:
        tool_msg = chunk["tools"]["messages"][0]
        print(f"\n📋 Observation: {tool_msg.content}")

print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("Done!")
print("=" * 60)

← Previous07.1 · The Agentic Loop — Tool Calling, MCP→ Next07.3 · Agentic Memory + Evaluation & Observability
07.3Chapter 7 · From RAG to AI Agents

Agentic Memory + Evaluation & Observability

Bina memory ke agent ek stateless completion engine hai — har turn pehle jaisa hi naya lagta hai. Memory hi woh capability hai jo agent ko personal, continuous aur efficient banati hai. Lekin memory persist karte hi agent ek transient tool se permanent data steward ban jata hai — aur uske saath governance, privacy aur security ki zimmedariyan aati hain. Isi liye memory aur observability ko saath me samajhna zaroori hai: ek batata hai agent ko kya yaad rakhna hai, dusra batata hai ki agent ne yaad karke kya kiya.

Short-term vs long-term memory

  • Short-term / working memory: Ye sirf current reasoning session ke dauraan information store karti hai. Iske bina agent pronouns samajh nahi sakta, multistep chain of thought maintain nahi kar sakta, aur single session ke andar errors correct nahi kar sakta. Example: user do turns pehle jis flight ka zikr kar raha tha, "it" se usi flight ko refer kar raha hai — bina short-term memory ke agent ye link nahi bana sakta. Production systems me ye aksar conversation history ki sliding window se handle hoti hai.
  • Long-term memory: Ye ek session se aage persist karti hai, aksar databases ya vector stores me implement hoti hai. Example: agent ko yaad rahe ki user window seats prefer karta hai, ya uski dietary restrictions kya hain — chahe ye baatein hafton pehle discuss hui hon. Long-term memory additive capability hai — ise tab implement karo jab agent ki value cumulative honi chahiye dinon, hafton ya mahino me, aur user ko "jaanna" (coding style, dietary restrictions, past project history) future interactions ka friction significantly kam karta ho. Lekin transactional agents ke liye — jaise one-off insurance claims chatbot — long-term memory aksar unnecessary hai; persistent storage avoid karne se privacy risks minimize hote hain aur data-handling compliance simplify hoti hai.

Memory tezi se har AI agent ki key capability ban rahi hai, kyunki ye teen cheezein deti hai: personalization (agent behavior user ki past actions ke hisaab se tailor hota hai), continuity (agent pichhli interactions "yaad" rakhta hai, jisse future tasks naturally flow karte hain), aur efficiency (agent wahi sawal dobara nahi poochta ya tools se information dobara gather nahi karta).

Implementation — memory with agentic RAG

Memory implement karna sirf logs ko database me dump karna nahi hai — iske liye active management strategy chahiye taaki agent sahi time par sahi information retrieve kare. Agentic RAG me do types hain:

  • Session-based storage (short-term): Implementation aksar simple hoti hai — session-specific database me interaction strings ki list. Coding agents ke liye file-based memory bhi traction gain kar rahi hai, jahan local project files agent ke environment ke liye persistent context provide karti hain. Ek common practice hai session consolidation: periodically agent session ko review karke key facts ka "compressed" summary banata hai (jaise "User prefers window seats") aur historical session context ko replace kar deta hai — isse retrieval accuracy improve hoti hai aur raw logs search karne ke comparison me token costs kam hote hain.
  • Semantic search and retrieval (long-term): Long-term memory semantic search par rely karti hai (jaise vector store use karke). Jab user sawal poochhta hai, to agent semantic search karke sabse relevant historical "memories" retrieve karta hai. Ye phir automatically agent ki current working memory (active context) me insert ho jati hain — current query aur relevant short-term memory ke saath. Short-term session history (ya session summaries) aur deep semantic retrieval ko balance karke aise agents banaye ja sakte hain jo contextually sharp rehte hain bina historical noise se overwhelm hue.

Enterprise guardrails — privacy aur integrity

Session-based storage aur semantic retrieval ka combination sophisticated agent experiences ki cognitive foundation deta hai, lekin ye sensitive interactions ka permanent record bhi banata hai. Enterprise environment me memory architecture ko teen critical risks address karne chahiye:

  • Governance and privacy: GDPR ya CCPA comply karne ke liye compliance deletion implement karni padti hai — aisi architecture jahan specific user ID se associated saari memories ko programmatically purge kiya ja sake. Iske alawa ek redaction layer use ki ja sakti hai jo sensitive PII ko scrub kar de, long-term vector store me commit hone se pehle hi.
  • Memory poisoning: Risk hai ki agent galat ya malicious information store kar le — jaise ek prompt injection jo kehta ho ki company ki nayi policy hai saare invoice disputes ko ek malicious URL par "verification" ke liye route karna — aur phir agent saare invoice disputes ko usi URL par redirect karne lage. Isse rokne ke liye validation gate use karo: ek secondary, lightweight LLM process jo potential memory ko persist karne se pehle evaluate karta hai — ye factual hai, safe hai, aur rakhne layak hai ya nahi.
  • Data lifecycle (decay): Information ki shelf life hoti hai. Decay policy implement karo taaki outdated memories (jaise saalon purana travel destination) eventually expire ya archive ho jayein — agent ka source of truth relevant aur legally compliant bana rahe. Aakhir me, information ko long-term persist karne ka decision is baat se govern hona chahiye ki woh reusable hai ya sirf transitional.

Agent evaluation — naye failure modes

Agents ko production me deploy karte waqt samajhna zaroori hai ki deterministic predecessors (1990s aur 2000s ke rules-based agents) ke opposite, inke failure modes systemic aur behavioral hote hain — kisi specific line of faulty code se trace hone wale traditional software bugs nahi, balki agent ki complexity aur nondeterministic LLM ki inherent role se paida hone wale issues. Main failure modes hain:

  • Tool hallucination: Tool agent ko inaccurate information deta hai aur agent bina verification ke use accept kar leta hai. Example: RAG tool galat response return kare, ya text2SQL tool user ke sawal ke liye galat SQL statement banaye — aur agent us par blindly bharosa karke kharab jawab de. Failure tool output par blind reliance aur use karne se pehle validation ki kami se aata hai.
  • Response hallucination: Tools sahi information dete hain, lekin agent response generate karte waqt use misuse ya distort kar deta hai. Issue tool me nahi, agent ke processing me hai — final output LLM se generate hota hai, isliye excellent tool outputs ke baad bhi output hallucinate ho sakta hai (jaise naive RAG me).
  • Goal misinterpretation: Agent user ke sawal ko galat samajhta hai aur intended task ke bajaye related lekin 100% correct nahi result deta hai. Example: ek sheher ka travel plan maanga gaya ho aur agent dusre sheher ka plan bana de.
  • Plan generation failures: Agent task ke liye actions ki sequence banata hai, lekin woh galat hoti hai — steps out of order, incomplete, ya generally flawed. Example: logon ki availability check karne se pehle meeting schedule kar dena. Plan surface par logical lagta hai lekin practice me kaam nahi karta.
  • Incorrect tool use: Agent galat tool select karta hai ya sahi tool ko invalid ya inaccurate arguments ke saath use karta hai. Example: emails ko archive karne ke bajaye delete kar dena, ya email galat recipient ko bhej dena. Ye risk tools ko diye gaye permissions aur access controls se heavily influence hota hai — read-only access wala tool emails ko analyze ya summarize kar sakta hai, lekin agent ki kisi bhi logic error ke bawjood unhe delete karne ki technical capability hi nahi rakhta. Read aur write access ke beech strict boundary define karke developers ensure kar sakte hain ki LLM ke poor decision ke baad bhi galti ka "blast radius" limited rahe.
  • Verification and termination failures: Agent ko pata nahi chalta ki task kab complete hua — woh bahut jaldi ruk jata hai (sirf partial result dekar) ya kabhi rukta hi nahi (same steps endlessly repeat karta hai). Dono cases me agent isliye fail hota hai kyunki woh user ki requirements ke hisaab se task completion ko properly judge nahi kar pata.
  • Prompt injection: End user deliberately aisa query deta hai jo agent ke intended behavior ko override karne ke liye design ki gayi ho — jaise safety rules ignore karwana ya purpose se bahar ke tasks karwana, jisse confidential information leak ho sakti hai. Ye failure serious hai kyunki agent manipulation ke liye vulnerable ho jata hai.

Agentic observability — "glass box" banana

Traditional observability tools deterministic systems ke liye bane hain — CPU aur memory utilization, network throughput, application error rates, request latency. Inki assumption hai ki operational stability se functional correctness infer ki ja sakti hai. AI agents ke saath ye assumption poori tarah toot jati hai: ek agent operationally "healthy" ho sakta hai — low CPU, low latency, zero system errors — aur phir bhi apne intended task me fail kar raha ho. Is disconnect ne AI agent observability naam ka naya paradigm paida kiya hai.

Agentic observability ka core hai agent ke complete end-to-end behavior ko monitor, samajh aur analyze karna — uski internal reasoning, decision-making processes, aur tools ke saath interactions (directly ya MCP servers ke through) samet. Ye observability ke teen traditional pillars — metrics, logs aur traces — par build hoti hai, aur do nayi capabilities add karti hai: evaluations (agent apna task kitna achha kar raha hai, ye qualitative aur quantitative assessment) aur governance (agent safely aur prescribed boundaries ke andar operate kar raha hai ya nahi, ye rules aur policies ka framework). Ultimate goal transparency hai — agent ko inscrutable "opaque box" se intelligible "glass box" me transform karna. Bina iske aap failures ke root causes par guess karte rehte hain, aur mission-critical applications me autonomous systems ko responsibly deploy nahi kar sakte.

Tracing — cornerstone technique

Observability ke saare components important hain, lekin tracing agent behavior samajhne ki cornerstone technique hai. Ek trace ek single request ke entire execution flow ko capture karta hai — initial user input se final output tak — structured, hierarchical series of events ke roop me jinhe spans kehte hain. Har span workflow ke andar discrete unit of work represent karta hai, jaise reasoning ke liye LLM call, RAG tool ki query, ya text2SQL tool ki call. In (potentially nested) spans ko visualize karke developers kisi bhi interaction ke liye agent ki chain of thought ko reconstruct aur analyze kar sakte hain. Ye step-by-step view debugging aur optimization ke liye invaluable hai — ye seedhe jawab deta hai: har reasoning step par LLM ko exact prompt kya bheja gaya tha? Agent ne kaunsa tool kin parameters ke saath call karne ka decision liya? Tool ne kya data return kiya aur agent ne use kaise interpret kiya? Har step me kitna time laga aur latency bottlenecks kahan hain?

Example: best flight dhoondhne ka task diya gaya agent search_flights tool ko kharab arguments ke saath call kare aur paanchvi try me succeed ho — final output ka simple log ye inefficiency reveal nahi karega, lekin trace me multiple sequential search_flights spans saaf dikh jayenge. Tracing performance issues bhi uncover karti hai — har span ki duration dekh kar pata chal sakta hai ki 22-second total response time chaar tools ki chain me ek slow API call ki wajah se tha.

Agentic observability metrics — kya measure karein

Traces individual executions ka qualitative, deep view dete hain; metrics time ke saath agent performance ka quantitative, aggregate view dete hain. AI-specific metrics traditional system health se aage jaakar behavior, quality aur resource consumption measure karte hain:

  • Token usage: Sabse critical operational metrics me se ek — LLM providers zyadaatar foundation models ko per-token basis par price karte hain, isliye har LLM call me consume hue input aur output tokens track karna cost monitor aur control karne ke liye essential hai. Kuch request types ke liye high token usage prompt design ya reasoning logic me inefficiency indicate kar sakta hai.
  • Inference latency: Agent ko response generate karne me kitna time lagta hai — aksar time-to-first-token (agent kitni jaldi respond karna shuru karta hai) aur end-to-end latency (poora response aane tak ka total time) me break down karke. Interactive applications me low latency positive user experience ke liye critical hai.
  • LLM and API call counts: Har task par core LLM aur external tools ko kitni calls ki gayin — workflow complexity aur efficiency ka measure. Simple task ke liye unexpectedly high calls kisi problem ka signal ho sakti hain, jaise agent loop me phans gaya ho ya convoluted reasoning path follow kar raha ho.
  • Tool call success/failure rate: Tools ke saath agent ki interactions ki reliability track karta hai. High failure rate tool me issue (API downtime), agent ki request format karne ki ability me problem, ya network issues indicate kar sakta hai.
  • Response quality: Agent ke responses ki "goodness" quantify karne wali broad category — hallucination rate (factually incorrect outputs ki frequency) aur accuracy, relevance aur helpfulness ke dusre measures. RAG metrics (Chapter 6) ke alawa agent evaluation ko additional dimensions capture karne chahiye: tool use efficiency (agent tools ko achhe se choose aur sequence karta hai ya nahi), multiturn coherence (extended multiturn sessions me context aur consistency kitni achhi maintain hoti hai), aur autonomy alignment (agent ke independent decisions abhi bhi user intent aur safety reflect karte hain ya nahi).
  • Human handoff rate: Kai applications me agent task ko human operator ko escalate kar sakta hai jab woh handle na kar paye. In handoffs ki frequency track karna agent ki capabilities ka direct measure hai aur ye reveal karta hai ki kis type ke queries ya tasks me woh struggle karta hai.

In metrics ko week-over-week ya month-over-month track karna important hai, taaki time ke saath changes aur regressions identify ho sakein.

Tools for agentic observability

Is space me pivotal development hai AI telemetry ka standardization OpenTelemetry (OTel) ke through — ek vendor-neutral, open source project jo applications ko instrument karne ke liye unified APIs, SDKs aur tools deta hai taaki telemetry data (traces, metrics, logs) generate aur export ho sake. OTel ke andar GenAI Special Interest Group (SIG) AI ke liye semantic conventions define kar raha hai — LLM calls, tool usage aur vector database queries jaise operations ko describe karne ki common language. Ye standardization critical hai: ye vendor lock-in prevent karta hai aur developers ko kisi bhi OTel-compatible framework se agents banakar telemetry kisi bhi OTel-compatible backend ko bhejne deta hai. Is open foundation par kai specialized platforms emerge hui hain: Langfuse (open source LLM engineering platform — detailed tracing, cost aur latency monitoring, prompt management, production traces se evaluation datasets banane ke tools); Arize Phoenix (OpenTelemetry par built open source platform — end-to-end visibility tracing se, aur routers, planners aur retrieval systems jaise agent components ke liye evaluation templates); LangSmith (LangChain framework se tightly integrated commercial platform — robust tracing aur debugging, prompts iterate karne ke liye collaborative "Playground", aur comprehensive evaluation framework). Vectara jaise AI agent platforms is level ki observability ko platform ke andar hi incorporate karte hain aur APIs ke through access dete hain.

Yaad rakho: Agent healthy dikh sakta hai aur phir bhi fail kar raha ho — CPU aur latency se correctness infer mat karo. Tracing se har span dekho, metrics se cost aur quality track karo, aur tools ko read-only rakh kar galti ka blast radius chhota karo. Memory persist karne se pehle hamesha poochho: ye reusable hai ya sirf transitional?
SOURCESource: Hands-On RAG for Production, O'Reilly, Chapter 7 — From RAG to AI Agents

08Chapter 8 · Multimodal RAG

Multimodal RAG — Tables + Images

Text-only RAG ek badi kami ke saath jeeta hai: enterprise data ka sabse valuable hissa aksar prose me nahi hota — woh financial table ki cell me, trend line ke curve me, ya chart ke andar chhupa hota hai. Bina chart dekhe, table padhe ya image samjhe, RAG system text documents par high-quality grounded answers de sakta hai, lekin jab accurate jawab ke liye zaroori information table ya image ke andar ho, to woh low-quality ya hallucinated responses deta hai. Multimodal RAG isi gap ko bharne ka naam hai — non-text modalities ko RAG me integrate karna.

Do approaches — conversion vs native

Production environment me "multimodal" ka matlab samajhne ke liye do categories helpful hain. Conversion approach me specialized parsers, automatic speech recognition (ASR), ya vision–language models (VLMs) se non-text data ko text-based structured representations me translate kiya jata hai, jo standard RAG stack me fit ho jayein. Native approach me multimodal LLMs alag modalities ke embeddings ko shared latent space me natively process karte hain. Sapna ek single native multimodal model ka hai jo raw audio aur video ko text jitni aasani se consume kare, lekin reality zyada complex hai. Is chapter ka focus conversion approach par hai, kyunki woh reliability aur observability ke liye abhi bhi industry standard hai — saath me native multimodal capabilities ki jhalak bhi di gayi hai jo in complex pipelines ko simplify karne lagi hain.

Tables kyun important hain

Zyadaatar enterprise environments me high-value documents me embedded tables hoti hain jo important information convey karti hain. Aas-paas ka text aksar narrative ya qualitative analysis deta hai, lekin tables khud distinct, semantic micro-documents hain jinme high-density, structured "source of truth" hoti hai. Financial sector me ek quarterly earnings report ka "results of operations" table revenue ko operating expenses se map karta hai. Supply chain aur manufacturing me bill of materials (BOM) table ek product unit banane ke liye hazaaron component parts, precise quantities aur vendor codes detail karta hai. Insurance aur healthcare me summary of benefits matrices procedure codes ko deductible limits aur copay amounts se cross-reference karti hain — provider aur beneficiary ke beech binding contract ki tarah kaam karti hain. Har industry me tables extremely valuable information rakhti hain, lekin unme structural complexity bhi hoti hai: irregular row heights, logic hierarchies me merged cells, aur specific footnotes — information-rich lekin computationally difficult components.

Tables extract karna — teen steps

Tables ko RAG flow me properly integrate karne ka pehla step hai unhe digital format me extract karna. Isme teen distinct steps hote hain:

  • Table extraction: Table ko surrounding document layout se alag entity ke roop me identify karna. Ye aksar vision model se hota hai — gridlines, alignment patterns aur distinct whitespace channels jaise visual cues scan karke. Phir internal grid topology map ki jati hai: row aur column separators identify karna (borderless tables me bhi) aur merged cells ya spanning headers jaise complex features ko correctly handle karna. Agar ye digital skeleton flawed ho, to baad ki text extraction jumbled ho jayegi — isliye system ko character contents padhne se pehle hi cell boundaries rigorously define karni padti hain. Kuch cases me tables 90 degrees clockwise rotated bhi hoti hain, jisse extraction aur bhi challenging aur kam accurate ho jata hai.
  • OCR and semantic interpretation: Physical grid establish hone ke baad, standard left-to-right text scanning ke opposite, yahan optical character recognition processing cell-by-cell content extract karti hai taaki ek column ka data dusre column me bleed na kare. Lekin raw text sirf characters ki string hai — system ko semantic classification apply karke text ka role determine karna padta hai: layout analyze karke header rows ko data rows se distinguish karna, aur key columns identify karna jo measured entities define karte hain.
  • Normalization: Extracted content ko clean, dataframe-like format me transform karna. Raw strings me aksar noise hota hai — currency symbols ya "$ (1,000)" jaise formatting — jinhe strip ya standardize karke clean numerical values banana padta hai.

In steps ko commercial services ya open source software se implement kiya ja sakta hai. Commercial managed services scanned documents, images ya handwriting ke liye great choice hain, jahan powerful OCR chahiye hota hai: Amazon Textract strong industry standard mana jata hai, Azure Document Intelligence aur Google Cloud Document AI strong alternatives hain. Ye sirf API calls ke roop me available hain, isliye inhe scanned, very high-value documents ke liye reserve karna behtar hai jahan cloud call ki extra cost aur latency superior OCR se justify ho. On-premises ya air-gapped environment me (bina outside access ke) ye services available nahi ho sakti. LlamaParse ek aur recent option hai jo PDF, PPTX aur dusre formats support karta hai, text, tables, images/diagrams extract karke Markdown me output deta hai — code open source hai lekin ye LlamaCloud ki commercial offering hai.

Open source libraries locally free chalti hain aur "native" digital files ke liye aksar behtar choice hain. IBM ka Docling aur Unstructured AI/LLM workflows ke liye design kiye gaye packages hain — complex structural understanding me excel karte hain, jaise merged cells aur table headers preserve karke unhe RAG pipelines ke liye clean JSON ya HTML formats me convert karna. Gmft exclusively table extraction me specialize karta hai — merged cells, multilevel headers aur image-based tables support karta hai. Ye local tools air-gapped deployments ya high-volume processing ke liye primary choice hain, jahan cloud API costs prohibitive ho jayenge.

Book me Docling se ek reinforcement learning textbook ki PDF parse karke table extract karne ka example hai: table ko dataframe me export karne par programs, hidden units, training games, opponents aur results wali ek proper table milti hai. Lekin usi document ki 11th table extract karne par output (0,0) aata hai — Docling us table ko properly extract karne me fail ho jata hai. Lesson: Docling highly capable hai, phir bhi table extraction document processing ke sabse difficult tasks me se ek hai. Layout complexity, merged cells aur borderless tables ke kaaran aksar empty objects ya misaligned columns milte hain — aur ye lagbhag saare competing commercial ya open source solutions par apply hota hai. Isliye production me kabhi 100% accuracy assume mat karo, aur raw parser output ko bina validation ke "source of truth" mat mano. Pragmatic approach hai: ek ya do tools select karke apne specific documents ke representative sample par chhota evaluation harness chalao, jahan output ko manually verify kar sako. Accuracy samajh aane ke baad hi production me implement karo. Advanced production environments me multiple table extraction libraries support karke har file ke liye sahi wali choose karna bhi common hai — one size fits all nahi hota, isliye document type ya use case ke hisaab se best extraction capability use karne wala conditional pipeline design karo.

Naive chunking tables ke liye kyun fail hoti hai

Table extract ho jaye, to bhi use normal text ki tarah chunk aur embed nahi kiya ja sakta. Ek simple product specification table lo — columns Product, Price (USD), Price (EUR), Rating; rows Model-A ($299, 4.5 stars), Model-B ($449, 4.2 stars), Model-C ($199, 3.9 stars), Model-X ($899, 4.8 stars), aur aakhir me Model-Titan ($1999, 4.9 stars). Agar is table ko Markdown text me convert karke LangChain ke RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter se chhote chunks (chunk size 100) me todo, to pehla chunk correctly header row capture karta hai, lekin har subsequent chunk "headless" hota hai — sirf do rows, bina header ke. Jab user poochhta hai "Model-X ki price kya hai?", to retrieval system sirf woh headless chunk pull kar sakta hai jisme "Model-X" match hota hai. LLM ko phir text milta hai "Model-X | $899 | 774.77 | 4.8 Stars" — bina is context ke ki har value ka matlab kya hai. Data aur uske column name ke beech ka critical link sever ho gaya hai, kyunki header dusre chunk me hai. Chunking se context ka loss hota hai — isliye tables ko alag tareeke se process karna padta hai.

Tables ko RAG ke liye process karna — structured context

Proper processing ke liye common practice hai table ko JSON structure me convert karna (Markdown bhi great option hai): table ko rows ki list ke roop me represent karo, jahan har row ek dictionary ho — column names keys, cell values values. Agla step hai is table ko LLM ko bhejkar uske content ki comprehensive summary maangna, aur summary ko ek special type ka chunk store karna jo full table contents ki taraf point karta hai. Query time par, agar summary chunk query ke liye relevant mana jaye, to full table pull karke complete table ko generative LLM ke context me provide kiya jata hai.

Ye recommended design pattern hai: tables ko structured context (JSON ya dataframes) ki tarah treat karo, raw text me flatten karne ke bajaye. Headers aur cells ke beech ka relationship structured format me preserve karne se model har cell ke liye full context maintain karta hai. RAG prompt me context items dynamically format kiye jate hain: normal facts text strings ki tarah, table information formatted JSON ke roop me (columns ke saath), aur generic structured data JSON serialization ke saath. Agar table bahut lambi ho to truncate karo lekin headers rakho, aur truncation note add karo. Modern LLMs code, JSON aur dataframe formats par extensively train hue hain, isliye ye pattern highly effective hai. Ek caveat: ye assume karta hai ki table modern LLM context limit me fit hone ke liye kaafi chhoti hai. Truly massive tables ke liye solution typically data-dependent hota hai — jaise appropriate ho to table ke columns filter karna.

Multi-page tables — stitching

Tables aksar ek page par khatm nahi hoti — woh kai pages me faili hoti hain. Is fragmentation se do distinct problems paida hoti hain: redundancy (har page par header repeat hota hai) aur ambiguity (pata nahi chalta ki agle page ki rows pichhle page ki continuation hain ya nayi table). Book ke example me ek badi table 6 pages me banti hui mili — har page par lagbhag 38–40 rows, total 205 rows. Solution hai tables ko stitch karna: consecutive pages se extract ki hui tables ko row counts ke hisaab se jodna (page 1 + 2 → 78 rows, phir + 3 → 116 rows, aur aise aage, aakhir me 205 rows). Stitching se pehle headers ko deduplicate karna aur row continuity verify karna padta hai, warna retrieval me duplicate ya incomplete tables milengi.

Documents with embedded images — teen approaches

Images ke saath bhi wahi principle hai: visual information ko aise represent karo ki retrieval pipeline use samajh sake. Teen approaches hain, jo fidelity aur cost ke spectrum par hain:

  • Image summarization: Ingestion phase me har image ko ek capable vision–language model (jaise GPT-5, Gemini 3, ya Claude 4.5) se pass karke 4–6 sentences ki concise lekin comprehensive summary generate karo — main subject ki detailed description, diagrams ya graphs ke liye conveyed information, trends aur conclusions, flowcharts/schemas ko aise describe karo ki description padhkar human diagram recreate kar sake, aur image me dikhne wala specific text context ke saath. Ye summary retrieval ke liye "chunk" ban jati hai, aur original image ko separately object store (jaise AWS S3) me store karke chunk ke metadata me reference link ya ID rakha jata hai. Query time par, agar image summary chunk relevant ho, to text-only generation model ko sirf summary context ke roop me di jati hai; VLM generation model ho to stored ID se original image retrieve karke actual image bytes (usually Base64 encoding me) context window me pass kiye jate hain — model image ko dobara "dekh" sakta hai, highest fidelity ke saath.
  • Raw image at query time (multimodal retrieval): Raw image ko query time par VLM ko pass karna highest detail preserve karta hai aur complex reasoning allow karta hai, lekin high-traffic production environments me ye zyada expensive, slower aur scale karna mushkil hota hai.
  • Shared embedding space: Neeche alag section me detail me.

Book me ek experiment hai: ek research report se GenBank base pairs ke growth ke baare me sawal poocha gaya. Text-only vector store (images ignore karke) ne weak jawab diya — expected, kyunki relevant information image (graph) me thi. Image summaries wale store ne behtar jawab diya — growth exponential thi, 1989 se 2000 tak substantially increase hui. Full images ke saath VLM ne best jawab diya — sirf "high growth" nahi, balki numbers bhi: lagbhag 1 billion se lagbhag 10 billion base pairs. Lesson saaf hai: summary reasoning ke liye kaafi hoti hai, lekin exact numbers jaise data-dense details ke liye original visual data chahiye hota hai. Implementation me LangChain ka MultiVectorRetriever use hota hai — summary documents vector store me hote hain, raw contents (image bytes) docstore me, aur retrieval ke baad doc_id se actual content fetch karke images aur texts ko alag karke VLM ko bheja jata hai.

Multimodal retrieval with a shared embedding space

Summarization approach ke opposite, shared embedding space approach images aur text ko directly ek hi vector space me map karta hai. Images aur text queries ko do alag languages ki tarah treat karo jo same underlying reality describe karti hain. Image ko English text me translate karne ke bajaye, multimodal embedding models — jaise OpenAI ka CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training), OpenCLIP, Google ka SigLIP (Sigmoid Loss for Language-Image Pre-training), Meta ka ImageBind, ya LanguageBind — dono modalities ko same embedding space me translate karte hain. Phir text query ka embedding image embeddings se compare karke retrieval hoti hai.

Book ke example me food images ke database par query chalayi gayi: "A round Margharitta Pizza" par top match ki probability 0.8323 mili — strong match. "Delicious italian food with cheese" jaise vague query par match probability sirf 0.0135 mili — system ko pata hai ki ye weak match hai. Ye probabilities absolute aur relative dono tareeke se interpret ki ja sakti hain. Shared embeddings ka fayda hai ki woh visual concepts aur aesthetics retrieve kar sakte hain jinhe text describe nahi kar sakta. Lekin do production frictions bhi hain: pehli, downstream reasoning mushkil ho jati hai — embedding se retrieve kiya hua image LLM ko "samjhana" padta hai, jo summarization approach me pehle se text me hota hai; dusri, multimodal embeddings aksar text embeddings se higher dimensionality use karte hain, jisse vector DB ka size badhta hai. Isliye summarization data-dense charts aur diagrams par reasoning ke liye essential hai, jabki shared embeddings visual concepts retrieve karne me excel karte hain — dono ke use cases alag hain.

Yaad rakho: Table ka structure hi uska meaning hai — header se alag ki hui row ka koi matlab nahi. Tables ko JSON/dataframe ki tarah structured context me rakho, images ko summary + original dono ke saath store karo, aur parser ki output par blind trust kabhi mat karo — apne documents par evaluation harness chalakar accuracy pehle verify karo.
audio-transcribe.ipynb — Audio Transcription for RAG — GitHub: ofermend/hands-on-rag, chapter8/audio-transcribe.ipynb (https://github.com/ofermend/hands-on-rag/blob/main/chapter8/audio-transcribe.ipynb)
import os
import json
import sys
from deepgram import DeepgramClient

deepgram_api_key = os.getenv("DEEPGRAM_API_KEY", None)
if not deepgram_api_key:
    print("Please setup your DeepGram API KEY")
    sys.exit(1)

# Multi-speaker call center audio (agent + customer discussing phone plan cancellation)
AUDIO_URL = "https://static.deepgram.com/examples/en_NatGen_CallCenter_BethTom_CancelPhonePlan.wav"

# Step 1: transcribe audio file
deepgram = DeepgramClient(api_key=deepgram_api_key)
response = deepgram.listen.v1.media.transcribe_url(
    url=AUDIO_URL,
    model="nova-2",
    smart_format=True,
    diarize=True,
    utterances=True
)

# Step 2: chunk transcription
chunks = []
current_chunk_text = []
current_chunk_meta = {"start": None, "end": None, "speakers": set()}
WORD_LIMIT = 512

# Extract utterances and arrange into chunks
utterances = response.results.utterances
for u in utterances:
    speaker = f"Speaker {int(u.speaker)}"
    text = u.transcript
    timestamp = u.start
    
    # Initialize start time for the new chunk if needed
    if current_chunk_meta["start"] is None:
        current_chunk_meta["start"] = timestamp
        
    # Add to current buffer
    current_chunk_text.append(f"{speaker}: {text}")
    current_chunk_meta["speakers"].add(speaker)
    current_chunk_meta["end"] = u.end  # Update end time continuously
    
    # Check simple length limit (rough word count approximation)
    current_word_count = sum(len(s.split()) for s in current_chunk_text)
    
    if current_word_count >= WORD_LIMIT:
        chunks.append({
            "content": "\n".join(current_chunk_text),
            "metadata": {
                "start_time": current_chunk_meta["start"],
                "end_time": current_chunk_meta["end"],
                "speakers": list(current_chunk_meta["speakers"])
            }
        })
        
        current_chunk_text = []
        current_chunk_meta = {"start": None, "end": None, "speakers": set()}

# Don't forget the last chunk if it has content
if current_chunk_text:
    chunks.append({
        "content": "\n".join(current_chunk_text),
        "metadata": {
            "start_time": current_chunk_meta["start"],
            "end_time": current_chunk_meta["end"],
            "speakers": list(current_chunk_meta["speakers"])
        }
    })

print(json.dumps(chunks, indent=2))

import os
import base64
import uuid
from pathlib import Path
from io import BytesIO
import requests
from typing import List, Dict, Any

from dotenv import load_dotenv
from PIL import Image

# LangChain 1.0+ imports
from langchain_chroma import Chroma
from langchain_huggingface import HuggingFaceEmbeddings
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langchain_classic.retrievers import MultiVectorRetriever
from langchain_classic.storage import InMemoryStore
from langchain_core.documents import Document
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnablePassthrough, RunnableLambda
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate

# Docling for PDF parsing
from docling.document_converter import DocumentConverter
from docling.datamodel.base_models import InputFormat
from docling.datamodel.pipeline_options import PdfPipelineOptions
from docling.document_converter import PdfFormatOption
from docling_core.types.doc import PictureItem

# OpenAI for image summarization
from openai import OpenAI as OpenAIClient

# Load environment variables
load_dotenv()

# Verify API key
if not os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"):
    raise ValueError("OPENAI_API_KEY not found in environment variables")

# Configuration
PDF_URL = "https://www.nlm.nih.gov/about/2014CJ_NLM.pdf"
PDF_PATH = "./data/2014CJ_NLM.pdf"
IMAGES_DIR = "./data/images"
CHROMA_DB_DIR = "./chroma_db"

# Create directories
Path("./data").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
Path(IMAGES_DIR).mkdir(exist_ok=True)

# Configure embeddings with local Qwen3
print("Loading Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B model from HuggingFace...")
embeddings = HuggingFaceEmbeddings(
    model_name="Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B",
    model_kwargs={'device': 'cpu', 'trust_remote_code': True},
    encode_kwargs={'normalize_embeddings': True, 'batch_size': 10}
)

# Initialize OpenAI client for image summarization
openai_client = OpenAIClient(api_key=os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"))

def download_pdf(url: str, save_path: str) -> str:
    """Download PDF from URL."""
    if os.path.exists(save_path):
        print(f"PDF already exists at {save_path}")
        return save_path
    
    print(f"Downloading PDF from {url}...")
    response = requests.get(url)
    response.raise_for_status()
    
    with open(save_path, 'wb') as f:
        f.write(response.content)
    
    return save_path

def parse_pdf_with_docling(pdf_path: str, images_dir: str) -> tuple:
    """Parse PDF with Docling and extract text, tables, and images."""
    
    print("Parsing PDF with Docling...")
    
    # Configure pipeline to generate picture images
    pipeline_options = PdfPipelineOptions()
    pipeline_options.images_scale = 2.0
    pipeline_options.generate_picture_images = True
    pipeline_options.generate_page_images = False
    
    # Create converter with format options
    converter = DocumentConverter(
        format_options={
            InputFormat.PDF: PdfFormatOption(pipeline_options=pipeline_options)
        }
    )
    
    # Convert the PDF
    result = converter.convert(pdf_path)
    
    # Get the document text
    doc_text = result.document.export_to_markdown()
    
    # Extract images with metadata
    images_data = []
    picture_counter = {}
    
    print("Extracting images from document...")
    for element, _level in result.document.iterate_items():
        if isinstance(element, PictureItem):
            page_num = element.prov[0].page_no if element.prov else 0
            
            if page_num not in picture_counter:
                picture_counter[page_num] = 0
            else:
                picture_counter[page_num] += 1
            
            filename = f"page_{page_num}_image_{picture_counter[page_num]}.png"
            filepath = os.path.join(images_dir, filename)
            image = element.get_image(result.document)
            
            if image:
                image.save(filepath, "PNG")                                
                images_data.append({
                    'ref': element.self_ref,
                    'page': page_num,
                    'local_path': filepath,
                    'filename': filename,
                    'position': element.prov[0].bbox.as_tuple() if element.prov else None
                })
                    
    return result, doc_text, images_data
